question: According to the World Health Organization, what is the primary focus of Primary Health Care along the health continuum?

options.A: Exclusively specialized hospital treatment and advanced surgeries
options.B: Health promotion, disease prevention, treatment, rehabilitation, and palliative care
options.C: Emergency trauma care in urban tertiary medical centers
options.D: Pharmaceutical research and drug manufacturing

explanation: PHC focuses on a continuum ranging from health promotion and disease prevention to treatment, rehabilitation, and palliative care. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T1#GNS124_U1_T1_h1)

question: Why is understanding Primary Health Care considered crucial for nursing students in Nigeria?

options.A: It shifts the healthcare focus exclusively to expensive tertiary facilities
options.B: It eliminates the need for community nurses in rural areas
options.C: It shifts the focus from hospital-centric curative medicine to community-based preventive care
options.D: It mandates that all nurses work only in private hospitals

explanation: PHC is important because it shifts the healthcare focus away from purely hospital-centric curative medicine toward community-based, preventive care. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T1#GNS124_U1_T1_h1)

question: In which year and location was the historic International Conference on Primary Health Care held?

options.A: 1990 in Geneva, Switzerland
options.B: 1978 in Alma-Ata, Kazakhstan
options.C: 1985 in Lagos, Nigeria
options.D: 2000 in New York, USA

explanation: The landmark International Conference on Primary Health Care took place in Alma-Ata, Kazakhstan, in 1978. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T1#GNS124_U1_T1_h2)

question: What primary global goal was famously associated with the Declaration of Alma-Ata in 1978?

options.A: Eradication of all known genetic disorders within a decade
options.B: Health for All by the Year 2000
options.C: Universal free university education for all health workers
options.D: Establishment of tertiary hospitals in every village

explanation: The Alma-Ata Declaration identified primary health care as the key to attaining the goal of 'Health for All by the Year 2000.' [learn more](GNS124_U1_T1#GNS124_U1_T1_h2)

question: Which core principle of PHC ensures that vulnerable and marginalized populations have fair access to health services?

options.A: Appropriate technology
options.B: Equitable distribution
options.C: Tertiary specialization
options.D: Centralized governance

explanation: Equitable distribution ensures that health services are shared fairly across all population groups, especially the vulnerable and marginalized. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T1#GNS124_U1_T1_h3)

question: Why is intersectoral collaboration considered a vital principle of Primary Health Care?

options.A: Because health is solely dependent on hospital doctors and nurses
options.B: Because other sectors like education and agriculture heavily influence the social determinants of health
options.C: To ensure that ministries of finance control all medical prescriptions
options.D: To eliminate the need for community involvement in healthcare planning

explanation: Intersectoral collaboration acknowledges that health is influenced by many factors outside the health sector, requiring cooperation with education, agriculture, and housing. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T1#GNS124_U1_T1_h3)

question: Which of the following is explicitly included as an essential component of Primary Health Care?

options.A: Advanced plastic and reconstructive surgery
options.B: Immunization against major infectious diseases
options.C: Commercial flight medical evacuation services
options.D: Genomic sequencing for rare genetic mutations

explanation: Immunization against major infectious diseases is one of the core essential components outlined in Primary Health Care frameworks. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T1#GNS124_U1_T1_h4)

question: What is the primary significance of the essential components of PHC for community health nurses?

options.A: They serve as a guide for delivering structured, comprehensive health services at the grassroots level.
options.B: They restrict nurses from providing any form of health education.
options.C: They apply exclusively to tertiary intensive care units.
options.D: They replace the need for nursing licensure examinations.

explanation: The essential components provide nurses with a standard package of services to deliver structured and comprehensive care at the grassroots level. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T1#GNS124_U1_T1_h4)

question: What is a major benefit of community participation in Primary Health Care initiatives?

options.A: It ensures that health programs are culturally acceptable, sustainable, and driven by local ownership.
options.B: It shifts all financial burdens exclusively onto international donors.
options.C: It removes the need for professional healthcare personnel in rural areas.
options.D: It centralizes all medical decision-making in urban federal capitals.

explanation: Community participation ensures local ownership, making health programs more culturally acceptable and sustainable. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T1#GNS124_U1_T1_h5)

question: Why must the health sector collaborate with agriculture and education to address childhood malnutrition?

options.C: Because health workers are not allowed to talk about food
options.A: Because food production and nutritional education fall under external sectors that impact overall health determinants
options.B: To increase the cost of medical consultations
options.D: To eliminate the need for primary health clinics

explanation: Intersectoral collaboration is necessary because agriculture and education directly influence food supply and nutritional knowledge, which are key health determinants. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T1#GNS124_U1_T1_h5)

question: Which agency is responsible for coordinating Primary Health Care at the national level in Nigeria?

options.A: Federal Ministry of Works and Housing
options.B: National Primary Health Care Development Agency (NPHCDA)
options.C: World Health Organization Regional Office
options.D: Medical and Dental Council of Nigeria

explanation: The National Primary Health Care Development Agency (NPHCDA) is charged with coordinating PHC policies and development nationally in Nigeria. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T1#GNS124_U1_T1_h6)

question: What is a common structural challenge affecting Primary Health Care centers in rural areas of Nigeria?

options.A: An overwhelming surplus of specialized neurosurgeons
options.B: Shortages of skilled personnel, poor infrastructure, and essential drug supply issues
options.C: Excessive funding leading to institutional inflation
options.D: Too many operational ambulances per clinic

explanation: Rural PHCs in Nigeria frequently struggle with poor infrastructure, a shortage of skilled workers, and unreliable essential drug supplies. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T1#GNS124_U1_T1_h6)

question: What is a major financial barrier that prevents low-income families from accessing care at primary health facilities in Nigeria?

options.A: Free universal medical services for everyone
options.B: High out-of-pocket spending for healthcare services and drugs
options.C: Mandatory state-funded health insurance coverage for all citizens
options.D: Excessive government subsidies on pharmaceuticals

explanation: High out-of-pocket spending forces families to pay directly for care, creating a major financial barrier and risking impoverishment. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T1#GNS124_U1_T1_h7)

question: How can task-shifting and task-sharing policies help mitigate workforce shortages in Nigerian Primary Health Care centers?

options.A: By allowing trained nurses and community health workers to safely deliver certain expanded lifesaving services
options.B: By restricting healthcare delivery exclusively to foreign specialist physicians
options.C: By shutting down primary health clinics to reduce staffing needs
options.D: By eliminating all clinical training requirements for nursing students

explanation: Task-shifting and task-sharing optimize the available workforce by empowering trained nurses and community health workers to provide expanded essential care. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T1#GNS124_U1_T1_h7)

question: What is considered the primary focus of Primary Health Care beyond disease treatment?

options.A: Expensive tertiary interventions
options.B: Wellness, disease prevention, and health promotion
options.C: Exclusive hospital-based care
options.D: Eliminating the nursing profession

explanation: PHC integrates health services deeply into the community, focusing on overall wellness, disease prevention, and health promotion alongside treatment. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T2#GNS124_U1_T2_h1)

question: Why is understanding Primary Health Care particularly vital for nursing students?

options.A: Nurses form the backbone of community-based health delivery.
options.B: It allows nurses to avoid working in hospitals entirely.
options.C: Nurses are solely responsible for global economic policies.
options.D: It prevents the need for clinical documentation.

explanation: Understanding PHC is essential because nurses form the backbone of community-based health delivery and advocate for health equity. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T2#GNS124_U1_T2_h1)

question: Which of the following best describes the pre-Alma-Ata medical model?

options.A: Community-centered and preventive
options.B: Curative, hospital-centric, and doctor-led
options.C: Equally distributed between rural and urban areas
options.D: Focused primarily on traditional herbal remedies

explanation: Before Alma-Ata, global healthcare was dominated by a rigid medical model prioritizing curative, hospital-centric, and doctor-led interventions. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T2#GNS124_U1_T2_h2)

question: What was a major consequence of the pre-Alma-Ata healthcare approach for rural populations?

options.A: Universal access to advanced surgeries
options.B: Severe health disparities and lack of basic services
options.C: Overfunding of local community clinics
options.D: Complete eradication of infectious diseases

explanation: Rural and impoverished populations suffered severe health disparities because resources were concentrated in elite urban medical facilities rather than community care. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T2#GNS124_U1_T2_h2)

question: In what year and city was the historic International Conference on Primary Health Care held?

options.A: 1990 in Geneva
options.B: 1978 in Alma-Ata
options.C: 2000 in Abuja
options.D: 1960 in New York

explanation: The conference was held in September 1978 in Alma-Ata, Kazakhstan, and produced the landmark Declaration of Alma-Ata. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T2#GNS124_U1_T2_h3)

question: What was the overarching global goal introduced by the Alma-Ata Declaration?

options.A: Health for All by the year 2000
options.B: Exclusive hospital care for urban elites
options.C: Elimination of all nursing schools
options.D: Privatization of international health systems

explanation: The declaration formally introduced PHC as the key to achieving 'Health for All' by the year 2000. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T2#GNS124_U1_T2_h3)

question: Which agency was established in Nigeria to coordinate PHC implementation and strengthen grassroots service delivery?

options.A: The National Primary Health Care Development Agency (NPHCDA)
options.B: The World Health Organization (WHO)
options.C: The Federal Ministry of Finance
options.D: The Nigerian Medical Association (NMA)

explanation: The NPHCDA was established to coordinate PHC implementation, streamline immunization programs, and strengthen grassroots service delivery in Nigeria. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T2#GNS124_U1_T2_h4)

question: What initiative in the late 1980s empowered Nigerian communities to manage basic drug supplies and health services?

options.A: The Alma-Ata Initiative
options.B: The Bamako Initiative
options.C: The Astana Declaration
options.D: The Lagos Health Scheme

explanation: The Bamako Initiative decentralized PHC governance and empowered local communities to manage and finance basic drug supplies through co-payments. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T2#GNS124_U1_T2_h4)

question: What was the primary characteristic of 'Selective Primary Health Care' introduced in the 1980s?

options.A: A focus on broad, comprehensive hospital construction
options.B: Targeted, vertical interventions like GOBI for specific health problems
options.C: The complete elimination of community health workers
options.D: Exclusive reliance on traditional herbalists

explanation: Selective PHC narrowed the broad Alma-Ata vision down to specific, cost-effective vertical interventions such as GOBI to tackle immediate child mortality. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T2#GNS124_U1_T2_h5)

question: Which Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) is specifically dedicated to health and well-being?

options.A: SDG Goal 1
options.B: SDG Goal 3
options.C: SDG Goal 8
options.D: SDG Goal 12

explanation: SDG Goal 3 is specifically dedicated to ensuring healthy lives and promoting well-being for all ages. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T2#GNS124_U1_T2_h5)

question: When and where was the Astana Declaration adopted to revitalize Primary Health Care?

options.A: 2018 in Kazakhstan
options.B: 1978 in Geneva
options.C: 2015 in New York
options.D: 1988 in Alma-Ata

explanation: The Astana Declaration was adopted in Kazakhstan in 2018, marking the 40th anniversary of the Alma-Ata conference. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T2#GNS124_U1_T2_h6)

question: Which of the following is emphasized as a key pillar of the Astana Declaration?

options.A: Abolishing community participation in healthcare
options.B: Making bold political choices for health across all sectors
options.C: Focusing solely on urban specialized hospitals
options.D: Eliminating preventative nursing programs

explanation: The Astana Declaration emphasizes making bold political choices for health across all sectors as one of its core pillars. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T2#GNS124_U1_T2_h6)

question: What is a major contemporary workforce challenge facing nursing practice in Nigeria today?

options.A: An extreme surplus of nursing graduates
options.B: Brain drain and severe staffing shortages
options.C: The complete absence of clinical duties
options.D: Excessive funding for local health centers

explanation: Nurses contend with systemic obstacles such as severe staffing shortages and brain drain, which impact healthcare delivery at the primary level. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T2#GNS124_U1_T2_h7)

question: What is a key future direction for nursing practice in Primary Health Care?

options.A: Eliminating community outreach entirely
options.B: Restricting nurses solely to administrative tasks
options.C: Expanding advanced practice nursing and nurse-led clinics
options.D: Stopping the use of all digital health technologies

explanation: Future directions emphasize advanced practice nursing and nurse-led clinics that allow nurses greater autonomy in managing care at the primary level. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T2#GNS124_U1_T2_h7)

question: Which international conference is widely recognized as the birthplace of the modern Primary Health Care strategy?

options.A: Abuja Declaration
options.B: Declaration of Alma-Ata
options.C: Ottawa Charter
options.D: Millennium Summit

explanation: The International Conference on Primary Health Care held in Alma-Ata in 1978 formulated the landmark Declaration of Alma-Ata, establishing PHC as the key to achieving Health for All. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T3#GNS124_U1_T3_h1)

question: What was the primary historical shift promoted by the adoption of Primary Health Care in 1978?

options.A: From hospital-based curative care to community-based preventative care
options.B: From government-funded health systems to entirely private healthcare
options.C: From rural health posts to highly specialized urban medical centers
options.D: From traditional medicine to advanced surgical procedures

explanation: PHC shifted the focus away from expensive, urban-centric, curative hospital care toward accessible, community-based preventative and promotive services. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T3#GNS124_U1_T3_h1)

question: Which PHC principle ensures that healthcare resources are distributed fairly based on need rather than the ability to pay?

options.A: Intersectoral collaboration
options.B: Equitable distribution
options.C: Appropriate technology
options.D: Curative specialization

explanation: Equitable distribution guarantees that health services are accessible to all population segments, particularly vulnerable and rural groups who need them most. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T3#GNS124_U1_T3_h2)

question: According to the philosophy of PHC, why is intersectoral collaboration necessary?

options.A: Because doctors alone cannot perform surgeries
options.B: Because health is influenced by factors outside the health sector, such as education and agriculture
options.C: To reduce the financial burden on international donor agencies
options.D: To eliminate the need for community health workers

explanation: Intersectoral collaboration acknowledges that health is determined by broad social factors, requiring coordinated action across sectors like education, agriculture, and housing. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T3#GNS124_U1_T3_h2)

question: How is equity in healthcare delivery best defined within the context of PHC?

options.A: Providing identical services to every single individual regardless of their health status
options.B: Allocating healthcare resources based on financial contribution
options.C: Ensuring equal access for equal need, reducing disparities among vulnerable groups
options.D: Focusing exclusively on urban populations with high disease burdens

explanation: Equity focuses on fairness, ensuring that people with equal health needs receive equal care and that resources are directed to reduce gaps for vulnerable populations. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T3#GNS124_U1_T3_h3)

question: What is the primary role of a nurse when applying the principle of social justice in Nigerian communities?

options.A: Advocating for marginalized groups and challenging systemic barriers to healthcare
options.B: Prioritizing wealthy patients who can pay for hospital maintenance
options.C: Limiting community access to reduce workload
options.D: Focusing solely on high-tech hospital interventions

explanation: Social justice in nursing involves advocating for vulnerable and marginalized populations to ensure they have fair access to health resources and human rights. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T3#GNS124_U1_T3_h3)

question: What is the primary benefit of genuine community participation in Primary Health Care programs?

options.A: It eliminates the need for professional nurses and doctors
options.B: It fosters local ownership and ensures long-term program sustainability
options.C: It shifts all financial responsibilities away from the government
options.D: It prevents the introduction of modern medicine

explanation: When communities actively participate in planning and implementing health programs, they develop a sense of ownership, which makes the programs much more sustainable. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T3#GNS124_U1_T3_h4)

question: Which of the following structures is commonly used in Nigeria to facilitate community participation at the grassroots level?

options.A: National Medical Association Board
options.B: Village Health Committees and Ward Development Committees
options.C: Private Pharmaceutical Council
options.D: International WHO Taskforce

explanation: Village Health Committees (VHCs) and Ward Development Committees (WDCs) are established in Nigeria to involve local communities directly in grassroots health planning and mobilization. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T3#GNS124_U1_T3_h4)

question: Why is intersectoral collaboration considered essential in achieving the goals of Primary Health Care?

options.A: Health is influenced by broader social and economic determinants outside the health sector
options.B: Doctors do not have enough time to manage community clinics alone
options.C: It is a mandatory requirement for international funding disbursement
options.D: It replaces the need for community health nurses

explanation: Intersectoral collaboration is necessary because health is shaped by factors like education, agriculture, housing, and sanitation, which require cooperation across multiple sectors. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T3#GNS124_U1_T3_h5)

question: Which combined intervention best demonstrates intersectoral collaboration in combating childhood malnutrition in a Nigerian community?

options.A: Prescribing multi-vitamins exclusively within the hospital pharmacy
options.B: Partnering with agricultural extension workers for food security while nurses provide nutritional education
options.C: Referring all malnourished children abroad for specialized treatment
options.D: Closing down local markets to regulate food prices

explanation: Partnering with agriculture to ensure food security alongside nursing education is a classic example of different sectors working together to solve a health-related problem. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T3#GNS124_U1_T3_h5)

question: What are the key defining characteristics of appropriate technology in Primary Health Care?

options.A: It must be imported from developed countries and require advanced engineering
options.B: It must be scientifically sound, culturally acceptable, and affordable using local resources
options.C: It focuses exclusively on advanced surgical interventions in tertiary hospitals
options.D: It relies entirely on traditional herbs without scientific testing

explanation: Appropriate technology must be scientifically valid, culturally appropriate, and financially sustainable using local resources available to the community. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T3#GNS124_U1_T3_h6)

question: Which of the following is a classic example of a cost-effective, appropriate technology intervention in child health?

options.A: Routine intravenous fluid therapy for every episode of mild diarrhea
options.B: Oral Rehydration Salts (ORS) and continued feeding for childhood diarrhea
options.C: Advanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in rural health posts
options.D: Imported specialized infant formulas for all newborns

explanation: ORS is a low-cost, scientifically proven, and easily administered appropriate technology that effectively prevents dehydration from diarrhea in community settings. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T3#GNS124_U1_T3_h6)

question: Which of the following best describes the multifaceted role of a nurse in implementing PHC in Nigeria?

options.A: Confining practice strictly to hospital-based surgical procedures
options.B: Acting as clinician, educator, community mobilizer, and advocate for vulnerable groups
options.C: Focusing exclusively on administrative paperwork in federal ministries
options.D: Acting as a passive observer in community health committees

explanation: Nurses in PHC play diverse roles including direct clinical care, health education, community mobilization, and advocating for vulnerable populations. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T3#GNS124_U1_T3_h7)

question: Who do primary health care nurses typically supervise and collaborate with at the grassroots level in Nigeria?

options.A: Consultant neurosurgeons and cardiologists
options.B: Community Health Extension Workers (CHEWs) and village health volunteers
options.C: Private pharmaceutical manufacturers
options.D: International trade diplomats

explanation: PHC nurses work closely with and supervise Community Health Extension Workers (CHEWs) and local volunteers to deliver grassroots healthcare services. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T3#GNS124_U1_T3_h7)

question: What is a major systemic challenge facing Primary Health Care implementation in Nigeria?

options.A: Excessive surplus of healthcare funding and resources
options.B: Chronic underfunding, poor infrastructure, and healthcare worker brain drain
options.C: Complete absence of community interest in health programs
options.D: Overabundance of rural health clinics with no patients

explanation: Chronic underfunding, poor infrastructure like roads and electricity, and the migration of health workers (brain drain) are major hurdles facing PHC in Nigeria. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T3#GNS124_U1_T3_h8)

question: What is required to improve the future prospects of PHC in Nigeria and overcome current challenges?

options.A: Abandoning community participation in favor of strictly hospital-based care
options.B: Strong political commitment, domestic resource mobilization, and staff capacity building
options.C: Eliminating all nursing roles in rural health centers
options.D: Relying solely on short-term foreign aid without government involvement

explanation: Revitalizing PHC requires strong political will, sustainable funding from domestic resources, and continuous training and support for healthcare workers. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T3#GNS124_U1_T3_h8)

question: In which year and location was the historic International Conference on Primary Health Care held?

options.A: 1948 in Geneva, Switzerland
options.B: 1978 in Alma-Ata, Kazakhstan
options.C: 1990 in Abuja, Nigeria
options.D: 2000 in Alma-Ata, Russia

explanation: The landmark International Conference on Primary Health Care took place in 1978 in Alma-Ata, Kazakhstan, establishing the global framework for health equity. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T4#GNS124_U1_T4_h1)

question: According to the Alma-Ata Declaration, how is health defined beyond the mere absence of disease?

options.A: As the ability to work productively without financial constraints
options.B: As a state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being
options.C: As access to modern pharmaceutical medications
options.D: As the total eradication of infectious diseases globally

explanation: The Alma-Ata Declaration defines health comprehensively as a state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being, recognizing it as a fundamental human right. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T4#GNS124_U1_T4_h1)

question: What is the primary goal of education concerning prevailing health problems in Primary Health Care?

options.A: To generate revenue for local health facilities
options.B: To empower individuals and communities with knowledge to take charge of their health
options.C: To train every community member to become a licensed nurse
options.D: To replace the need for curative medications completely

explanation: This PHC element aims to equip individuals and communities with health literacy so they can actively prevent and control health problems themselves. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T4#GNS124_U1_T4_h2)

question: How should health education be delivered to ensure maximum effectiveness in diverse communities?

options.A: Using complex medical jargon exclusively
options.B: Through rigid, standardized international lectures
options.C: In a culturally sensitive and locally appropriate manner
options.D: Only via digital smartphones and social media

explanation: For health education to foster real behavioral change, it must be culturally sensitive, contextually relevant, and tailored to the audience's background. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T4#GNS124_U1_T4_h2)

question: Which of the following is emphasized in PHC nutrition education for infants?

options.A: Early introduction of solid foods at two weeks of life
options.B: Exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of life
options.C: Complete reliance on imported powdered milk formulas
options.D: Restriction of fluid intake during weaning

explanation: Proper infant nutrition under PHC strongly promotes exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of life to protect against infections and malnutrition. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T4#GNS124_U1_T4_h3)

question: What is a primary purpose of growth monitoring and promotion (GMP) activities in primary healthcare settings?

options.A: To diagnose chronic adult cardiovascular diseases
options.B: To detect early signs of malnutrition and failure to thrive in children
options.C: To determine the exact adult height of community members
options.D: To calculate individual taxation rates based on weight

explanation: Growth monitoring helps healthcare workers track a child's development and catch early indicators of malnutrition before severe clinical complications arise. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T4#GNS124_U1_T4_h3)

question: Access to safe water and basic sanitation primarily helps prevent which category of diseases?

options.A: Genetic and inherited metabolic disorders
options.B: Waterborne and vector-borne infectious diseases
options.C: Degenerative neurological conditions
options.D: Occupational repetitive strain injuries

explanation: Safe water and sanitation directly target and prevent waterborne infections like cholera, typhoid, and dysentery, as well as related environmental illnesses. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T4#GNS124_U1_T4_h4)

question: What is a key benefit of promoting proper latrine use and eliminating open defecation in communities?

options.A: It increases agricultural soil salinity
options.B: It prevents environmental contamination and reduces diarrheal disease transmission
options.C: It eliminates the need for handwashing practices
options.D: It accelerates industrial waste breakdown

explanation: Proper sanitation facilities like latrines stop fecal contamination of soil and water sources, thereby interrupting the transmission cycle of dangerous pathogens. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T4#GNS124_U1_T4_h4)

question: What is a primary objective of integrating family planning within maternal and child health services?

options.A: To completely halt population growth nationwide
options.B: To help couples space pregnancies adequately and reduce maternal and infant mortality
options.C: To replace antenatal care visits for pregnant women
options.D: To provide specialized treatment for infectious diseases

explanation: Family planning allows adequate birth spacing, which significantly protects the health of both mother and child and lowers mortality rates. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T4#GNS124_U1_T4_h5)

question: Which specific prophylactic intervention is routinely administered to pregnant women during antenatal visits to prevent a neonatal killer disease?

options.A: Tetanus toxoid immunization
options.B: Rabies post-exposure prophylaxis
options.C: Inactivated polio booster shot
options.D: Anthrax antitoxin therapy

explanation: Pregnant women receive tetanus toxoid immunizations during antenatal care to protect both the mother and the newborn from neonatal tetanus. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T4#GNS124_U1_T4_h5)

question: How do vaccines primarily protect individuals and communities against infectious diseases?

options.A: By destroying human white blood cells permanently
options.B: By stimulating the immune system to produce protective antibodies without causing the disease
options.C: By altering human genetic material to resist all known pathogens
options.D: By acting as a direct antibiotic that kills bacteria in the gut

explanation: Vaccines introduce weakened or inactivated antigens to prompt antibody production safely, conferring immunity against future infections. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T4#GNS124_U1_T4_h6)

question: Why is maintaining the cold chain critically important during vaccine delivery and storage?

options.A: It ensures vaccines remain pleasant-tasting for young infants
options.B: It prevents vaccines from freezing solid and turning into gas
options.C: It preserves the biological potency and effectiveness of the vaccines
options.D: It allows vaccines to be stored at room temperature indefinitely

explanation: Temperature control via the cold chain is essential to maintain vaccine stability and potency so they can effectively trigger an immune response. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T4#GNS124_U1_T4_h6)

question: Which of the following interventions is a cornerstone in the prevention and control of malaria within endemic regions?

options.A: Routine administration of broad-spectrum antiviral pills to all adults
options.B: Distribution and utilization of insecticide-treated nets (ITNs)
options.C: Surgical removal of regional lymph nodes in infected children
options.D: Strict quarantine of entire communities during rainy seasons

explanation: Insecticide-treated nets are a proven, cost-effective vector control method used to prevent mosquito bites and malaria transmission. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T4#GNS124_U1_T4_h7)

question: What is a key responsibility of community health nurses regarding locally endemic diseases?

options.A: Conducting epidemiological surveillance and case tracking
options.B: Developing new pharmaceutical drugs in clinical laboratories
options.C: Imposing international travel bans on affected regions
options.D: Abolishing traditional healing practices entirely

explanation: Nurses monitor infection trends, conduct active case finding, and track disease patterns as part of local epidemiological surveillance efforts. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T4#GNS124_U1_T4_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of providing appropriate treatment for common diseases and injuries at the PHC level?

options.A: To handle complex neurosurgeries and organ transplants
options.B: To manage everyday health issues promptly at the grassroots level and prevent complications
options.C: To keep patients hospitalized for extended rehabilitation periods
options.D: To eliminate the need for any preventative health measures

explanation: Treating common conditions at the primary level ensures fast relief, prevents severe complications, and reduces unnecessary hospital referrals. [learn more](GNS124_U1_T4#GNS124_U1_T4_h8)

question: When a nurse encounters a patient at a primary health clinic with severe, life-threatening red-flag symptoms, what is the appropriate action?

options.A: Send the patient home without medication to see if they recover
options.B: Perform major surgical procedures immediately on-site

explanation: Schistosomiasis is commonly referred to as snail fever or bilharzia due to the snail vector involved in its life cycle. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h1)

question: Which demographic group is particularly vulnerable to the effects of schistosomiasis in Nigeria?

options.A: School-aged children
options.B: Neonates under 28 days
options.C: Postmenopausal women
options.D: Professional athletes

explanation: School-aged children, along with farmers and fishermen, are among the most frequently affected and vulnerable groups due to recreational and occupational water contact. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h1)

question: Which form of the parasite is responsible for penetrating human skin during water contact?

options.A: Miracidium
options.B: Cercaria
options.C: Metacercaria
options.D: Schistosomule

explanation: Free-swimming cercariae emerge from freshwater snails and actively penetrate the intact skin of humans wading, swimming, or working in infested water. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h2)

question: Which of the following serves as the intermediate host for Schistosoma parasites?

options.A: Freshwater snails
options.B: Blackflies
options.C: Female Anopheles mosquitoes
options.D: Tsetse flies

explanation: Freshwater snails belonging to genera such as Bulinus and Biomphalaria act as the essential intermediate host where the parasite undergoes asexual reproduction. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h2)

question: What primary human practice directly contaminates freshwater bodies with schistosome eggs?

options.A: Open defecation and urination near water
options.B: Boiling untreated river water
options.C: Using pit latrines far from water bodies
options.D: Wearing protective rubber boots

explanation: Open defecation and urination near or directly into water sources allow eggs from infected individuals to reach the water and hatch into miracidia. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h3)

question: Which of the following is a major occupational risk factor for acquiring schistosomiasis in Nigeria?

options.A: Working as a bank teller in an urban area
options.B: Fishing and rice farming in rural waterways
options.C: Long-distance truck driving on highways
options.D: Teaching in a secondary school classroom

explanation: Occupations involving prolonged, direct contact with freshwater such as fishing and rice farming significantly increase the risk of cercarial skin penetration. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h3)

question: What is the classic presenting symptom of chronic urinary schistosomiasis caused by Schistosoma haematobium?

options.A: Terminal hematuria
options.B: Jaundice
options.C: Profuse watery diarrhoea
options.D: Severe chest pain

explanation: Terminal hematuria, or blood appearing at the end of urination, is a hallmark clinical sign of urinary schistosomiasis caused by S. haematobium eggs damaging the bladder mucosa. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h4)

question: Katayama fever represents which phase of schistosomiasis?

options.A: Chronic terminal phase
options.B: Acute phase
options.C: Asymptomatic carrier phase
options.D: Post-treatment relapse phase

explanation: Katayama fever is the acute systemic hypersensitivity reaction that occurs weeks after initial cercarial penetration and parasite migration. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h4)

question: What is the gold standard diagnostic method for confirming intestinal schistosomiasis in routine clinical settings?

options.A: Chest X-ray
options.B: Stool microscopy using Kato-Katz technique
options.C: Complete blood count with differential
options.D: Urinalysis using chemical dipsticks only

explanation: Stool microscopy, particularly utilizing the Kato-Katz thick smear method, is the standard parasitological procedure for detecting S. mansoni eggs in feces. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h5)

question: When is the optimal time of day to collect a urine sample for detecting S. haematobium eggs?

options.A: Early morning fasting sample
options.B: Midday, following physical activity
options.C: Late evening before sleep
options.D: Any random time of the day

explanation: Urine collection is ideally performed around midday (typically between 10:00 AM and 2:00 PM) after physical exertion, as egg excretion reaches its peak during this period. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h5)

question: What is the primary drug of choice for treating all forms of schistosomiasis?

options.A: Metronidazole
options.B: Praziquantel
options.C: Albendazole
options.D: Chloroquine

explanation: Praziquantel is the safe and highly effective oral medication recommended globally and in Nigeria for treating infections caused by all Schistosoma species. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h6)

question: How does Praziquantel exert its therapeutic action against schistosomes?

options.A: By blocking folic acid synthesis
options.B: By inhibiting cellular respiration
options.C: By increasing cell membrane calcium permeability, causing paralysis
options.D: By dissolving the outer chitin shell of the egg

explanation: Praziquantel increases calcium permeability across the parasite's cell membrane, resulting in severe muscle contraction, paralysis, and death of the adult worms. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h6)

question: Which long-term malignancy is strongly associated with chronic untreated S. haematobium infection?

options.A: Squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder
options.B: Hepatocellular carcinoma
options.C: Renal cell carcinoma
options.D: Colorectal adenocarcinoma

explanation: Chronic inflammation and irritation from S. haematobium eggs in the bladder significantly elevate the risk of developing squamous cell carcinoma of the urinary bladder. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h7)

question: What pathological liver condition is caused by chronic S. mansoni egg deposition?

options.A: Biliary cirrhosis
options.B: Periportal fibrosis (Symmers pipe-stem fibrosis)
options.C: Fatty liver disease (steatosis)
options.D: Hepatic adenoma

explanation: Trapped S. mansoni eggs in the portal venules stimulate severe fibrosis around the portal tracts, known as Symmers pipe-stem fibrosis, leading to portal hypertension. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h7)

question: What is the primary goal of Mass Drug Administration (MDA) programs in schistosomiasis control?

options.A: To permanently immunize individuals against future infections
options.B: To reduce morbidity and parasite burden in high-risk communities
options.C: To destroy all freshwater snail breeding sites instantly
options.D: To treat acute bacterial coinfections

explanation: MDA aims to periodically treat populations at risk to control morbidity, reduce worm burdens, and prevent severe long-term complications in endemic regions. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h8)

question: Which PHC strategy directly prevents parasite eggs from entering local natural water sources?

options.A: Mass distribution of iron supplements
options.B: Constructing safe latrines to stop open defecation
options.C: Administering prophylactic antibiotics
options.D: Conducting routine blood pressure screenings

explanation: Building and utilizing safe latrines prevents open defecation and urination near water bodies, breaking the transmission cycle at its source. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T10#GNS214_U1_T10_h8)

question: What is the natural animal reservoir primarily responsible for circulating the Ebola virus before spillover into humans?

options.A: Domestic dogs
options.B: Fruit bats
options.C: Mosquitoes
options.D: Pigs

explanation: Fruit bats are recognized as the natural animal reservoirs for the Ebola virus before it spills over into the human population. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h1)

question: To which viral family does the Ebola pathogen belong?

options.A: Filoviridae
options.B: Coronaviridae
options.C: Retroviridae
options.D: Flaviviridae

explanation: The Ebola virus is a member of the Filoviridae family, characterized by filamentous viral particles. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h1)

question: Which of the following best describes the primary cellular targets of the Ebola virus?

options.A: Epithelial cells and neurons
options.B: Endothelial cells, macrophages, and hepatocytes
options.C: Osteocytes and chondrocytes
options.D: Red blood cells only

explanation: The virus primarily targets endothelial cells, mononuclear phagocytes (macrophages), and hepatocytes, driving systemic inflammation and coagulopathy. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h2)

question: How is the Ebola virus predominantly transmitted between humans?

options.A: Through droplet inhalation during normal breathing
options.B: Via mosquito and tick vectors
options.C: Through direct contact with infected bodily fluids or contaminated materials
options.D: By consuming thoroughly cooked bushmeat

explanation: Transmission occurs strictly through direct contact with blood, secretions, organs, or other bodily fluids of infected individuals and contaminated surfaces. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h2)

question: What is the typical incubation period range for the Ebola virus?

options.A: 1 to 3 hours
options.B: 2 to 21 days
options.C: 30 to 45 days
options.D: 6 months to 1 year

explanation: The incubation period for EVD ranges from 2 to 21 days, though most patients show symptoms within 8 to 10 days. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h3)

question: Which symptoms typically characterize the transition into the 'wet phase' of Ebola Virus Disease?

options.A: Profuse watery diarrhea, vomiting, and abdominal pain
options.B: Paralysis and chronic respiratory failure
options.C: Jaundice and severe pruritus
options.D: Pustular skin rashes over the trunk

explanation: The wet phase is marked by gastrointestinal symptoms like profuse diarrhea and vomiting, leading to rapid fluid volume loss. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h3)

question: What is the primary diagnostic laboratory test used to confirm Ebola Virus Disease?

options.A: Complete blood count with differential
options.B: Reverse Transcription-Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR)
options.C: Sputum acid-fast bacilli smear
options.D: Widal agglutination test

explanation: RT-PCR assay is the gold standard laboratory test used to detect viral RNA and confirm EVD in blood samples. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h4)

question: Why is early epidemiological triage critical during nursing assessment for EVD?

options.A: It cures the patient before symptoms appear
options.B: It allows immediate isolation and prevents further healthcare-associated transmission
options.C: It replaces the need for laboratory confirmation entirely
options.D: It guarantees access to mechanical ventilation

explanation: Immediate epidemiological triage identifies potential cases quickly, allowing nurses to enforce isolation protocols and prevent community or hospital outbreaks. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h4)

question: Why should NSAIDs like ibuprofen be avoided when managing a patient with suspected EVD?

options.A: They cause severe respiratory depression
options.B: They increase the risk of bleeding and hemorrhage
options.C: They neutralize the effects of rehydration salts
options.D: They render diagnostic RT-PCR tests inaccurate

explanation: NSAIDs impair platelet function and exacerbate the bleeding risks associated with Ebola-induced coagulopathy. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h5)

question: What is the primary goal of fluid management in EVD patients?

options.A: To increase blood pressure and correct severe hypovolemic dehydration
options.B: To flush the virus out of the kidneys rapidly
options.C: To induce diuresis and prevent renal failure
options.D: To dilute the concentration of red blood cells

explanation: Aggressive fluid resuscitation replaces massive fluid losses from vomiting and diarrhea, preventing fatal hypovolemic shock. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h5)

question: What role does the 'buddy system' play during PPE removal in an Ebola care setting?

options.A: It speeds up patient discharge procedures
options.B: It ensures a trained observer monitors the doffing process to prevent self-contamination
options.C: It provides emotional comfort to the healthcare worker
options.D: It replaces the need for chlorine disinfection

explanation: The buddy system involves an observer watching the doffing process step-by-step to catch and correct any accidental contamination errors. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h6)

question: Which concentration of chlorine solution is generally recommended for decontaminating environmental surfaces in EVD units?
explanation: A 0.5% chlorine solution is standard for disinfecting surfaces and medical equipment, whereas 0.05% is used for hand hygiene if soap is unavailable. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h6)

question: For how many days must a person identified as a contact of an EVD patient be actively monitored?

options.A: 5 days
options.B: 10 days
options.C: 21 days
options.D: 40 days

explanation: Contacts must be monitored for 21 days, matching the maximum incubation period of the Ebola virus. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of contact tracing during an Ebola outbreak?

options.A: To arrest individuals who violate quarantine rules
options.B: To identify exposed individuals early and monitor them for symptoms to halt transmission chains
options.C: To provide universal vaccination to the entire community
options.D: To collect taxes for public health infrastructure

explanation: Contact tracing ensures exposed persons are monitored so they can be isolated and treated immediately if symptoms arise, preventing further spread. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h7)

question: What is Post-Ebola Syndrome (PES)?

options.A: A recurrent acute infection that occurs exactly 5 years post-recovery
options.B: A constellation of chronic physical and psychological symptoms experienced by survivors
options.C: An acute viral mutation that makes the virus airborne
options.D: A permanent immunity booster acquired by family members

explanation: PES refers to the long-term physical and mental health issues, such as joint pain, fatigue, and depression, that persist in survivors. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h8)

question: In which body fluid can the Ebola virus persist for extended periods after a patient has clinically recovered?

options.A: Saliva
options.B: Sweat
options.C: Semen
options.D: Urine

explanation: The virus can persist in immunologically privileged sites like semen, posing a risk of sexual transmission long after recovery. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T11#GNS214_U1_T11_h8)

question: Which specific human receptor does the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein bind to in order to gain entry into host cells?

options.A: Beta-2 adrenergic receptor
options.B: Angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptor
options.C: CD4 helper T-cell receptor
options.D: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor

explanation: SARS-CoV-2 features surface spike glycoproteins that specifically bind to human angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) receptors to facilitate entry into host cells. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h1)

question: What is the typical incubation period range for COVID-19?

options.A: 1 to 3 hours
options.B: 2 to 14 days
options.C: 3 to 6 weeks
options.D: 2 to 4 months

explanation: The incubation period for COVID-19 typically ranges from 2 to 14 days, with a median of approximately 4 to 5 days. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h1)

question: What primary lung cells are initially targeted by SARS-CoV-2 during infection?

options.A: Alveolar epithelial type II cells
options.B: Goblet cells
options.C: Ciliated columnar cells
options.D: Pleural mesothelial cells

explanation: The virus primarily attaches to and infects alveolar epithelial type II cells in the lungs, leading to localized injury and inflammation. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h2)

question: What severe systemic immune complication is characterized by a massive release of pro-inflammatory cytokines like IL-6?

options.A: Anaphylactic shock
options.B: Cytokine storm
options.C: Septic rebound
options.D: Antigenic shift

explanation: A cytokine storm involves the excessive release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, leading to systemic hyperinflammation, endothelial injury, and ARDS. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h2)

question: Which of the following are recognized hallmark sensory symptoms of COVID-19?

options.A: Loss of hearing and blurred vision
options.B: Loss of taste (ageusia) and smell (anosmia)
options.C: Hyper-acusis and photophobia
options.D: Numbness and tingling in extremities

explanation: Loss of taste (ageusia) and loss of smell (anosmia) are classic, hallmark clinical manifestations frequently reported by COVID-19 patients. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h3)

question: An adult patient presents with a respiratory rate of 34 breaths per minute and an oxygen saturation of 90% on room air. Into which clinical stage does this patient fall?

options.A: Mild
options.B: Moderate
options.C: Severe
options.D: Asymptomatic

explanation: Severe illness is indicated by an oxygen saturation of less than 93% on room air or a respiratory rate greater than 30 breaths per minute. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h3)

question: What is considered the gold standard diagnostic test for confirming SARS-CoV-2 infection?

options.A: Complete blood count (CBC)
options.B: Chest X-ray
options.C: Reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR)
options.D: Rapid antigen test (RDT)

explanation: RT-PCR molecular testing of nasopharyngeal swabs is the gold standard for confirming the presence of SARS-CoV-2 RNA. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h4)

question: What is the primary purpose of immediate triage at the entrance of a primary health care facility?

options.A: To collect upfront consultation fees
options.B: To identify and isolate suspected cases to prevent transmission
options.C: To administer prophylactic antibiotics to everyone
options.D: To immediately discharge asymptomatic visitors

explanation: Immediate triage allows clinics to quickly identify, mask, and isolate suspected COVID-19 cases, preventing nosocomial spread among staff and patients. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h4)

question: What non-pharmacological nursing intervention can significantly improve oxygenation in conscious, non-intubated patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure?

options.A: Supine flat resting
options.B: Awake prone positioning
options.C: Trendelenburg positioning
options.D: High Fowler's position exclusively

explanation: Awake prone positioning (lying on the stomach) helps improve ventilation-perfusion matching and oxygenation in conscious patients with respiratory compromise. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h5)

question: Which medication class is routinely administered to hospitalized COVID-19 patients requiring supplemental oxygen to reduce systemic inflammation?

options.A: Corticosteroids (e.g., dexamethasone)
options.B: Loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide)
options.C: Beta-blockers (e.g., atenolol)
options.D: Proton pump inhibitors (e.g., omeprazole)

explanation: Corticosteroids like dexamethasone are standard of care to reduce the harmful systemic inflammatory response and mortality in oxygen-requiring patients. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h5)

question: What term is used to describe persistent symptoms that continue or develop weeks or months after the acute COVID-19 infection has resolved?

options.A: Acute rebound syndrome
options.B: Long COVID / PASC
options.C: Post-viral secondary sepsis
options.D: Chronic respiratory failure

explanation: Long COVID or post-acute sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (PASC) refers to symptoms that persist or develop long after acute illness recovery. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h6)

question: Which of the following is a recognized thromboembolic complication associated with COVID-19?

options.A: Iron deficiency anemia
options.B: Pulmonary embolism
options.C: Gouty arthritis
options.D: Osteoporosis

explanation: COVID-19 induces a hypercoagulable state, putting patients at high risk for complications such as pulmonary embolism and deep vein thrombosis. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h6)

question: Which type of respirator mask is specifically required when performing aerosol-generating procedures (AGPs) on COVID-19 patients?

options.A: Cloth face mask
options.B: Simple surgical mask
options.C: N95 respirator
options.D: Clear plastic face shield alone

explanation: N95 or equivalent particulate respirators provide the necessary airborne protection when performing aerosol-generating procedures. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h7)

question: What is the most critical first step before and after touching a patient or their immediate environment?

options.A: Applying sterile gloves without washing hands
options.B: Performing proper hand hygiene
options.C: Changing the surgical gown
options.D: Spraying disinfectant in the air

explanation: Hand hygiene using soap and water or alcohol-based hand sanitizer is the single most effective baseline measure for preventing pathogen transmission. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h7)

question: What is the primary public health goal of vaccination against COVID-19?

options.A: To completely eradicate viral mutations globally within weeks
options.B: To prevent severe disease, hospitalization, and death
options.C: To eliminate the need for any future hand hygiene
options.D: To cause mild infection in all healthy adults

explanation: While breakthrough infections can occur, vaccines are primarily designed and proven to protect individuals from severe illness, hospitalization, and death. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h8)

question: What key nursing activity helps combat vaccine hesitancy in local Nigerian communities?

options.A: Mandatory isolation of unvaccinated citizens
options.B: Culturally sensitive communication and community leader engagement
options.C: Withholding primary healthcare services from hesitant individuals
options.D: Avoiding discussions about vaccine side effects

explanation: Engaging community leaders and delivering culturally sensitive education builds trust and effectively addresses vaccine hesitancy. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h8)

question: What is the primary characteristic of diabetes mellitus?

options.A: Persistent hypoglycemia
options.B: Persistent hyperglycemia
options.C: Excessive insulin production
options.D: Normal blood glucose levels

explanation: Diabetes mellitus is characterized by persistent high blood sugar, known as hyperglycemia, caused by insulin defects. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h1)

question: What is a key responsibility of nurses in the Nigerian primary health care setting regarding diabetes?

options.A: Performing complex surgical interventions
options.B: Providing culturally appropriate lifestyle counseling and early detection
options.C: Manufacturing insulin locally
options.D: Restricting patients from eating local foods entirely

explanation: Nurses in PHC clinics serve on the frontline to recognize symptoms early and provide relevant lifestyle counseling to patients. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h1)

question: Which type of diabetes involves autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells leading to absolute insulin deficiency?

options.A: Type 2 diabetes
options.B: Gestational diabetes
options.C: Type 1 diabetes
options.D: Secondary diabetes

explanation: Type 1 diabetes is characterized by the autoimmune destruction of beta cells, causing an absolute lack of insulin. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h2)

question: How is Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) defined?

options.A: Diabetes diagnosed before pregnancy
options.B: Any degree of glucose intolerance recognized for the first time during pregnancy
options.C: A permanent form of Type 1 diabetes occurring in pregnant women
options.D: Insulin resistance caused by lactation

explanation: GDM is specifically defined as glucose intolerance that is first recognized during the gestational period. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h2)

question: Which of the following is a key contributor to rising diabetes risk factors in Nigerian urban areas?

options.A: Excessive physical farming
options.B: Rapid urbanization and dietary shifts
options.C: High consumption of raw green vegetables
options.D: Universal access to fitness centers

explanation: Urbanization brings lifestyle shifts and diets rich in refined carbohydrates, increasing diabetes risk factors. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h3)

question: What are the classic triad of symptoms frequently seen in patients presenting with diabetes?

options.A: Polyuria, polydipsia, and polyphagia
options.B: Hypertension, fever, and rash
options.C: Bradycardia, hypotension, and lethargy
options.D: Constipation, jaundice, and oliguria

explanation: The classic triad consists of excessive urination (polyuria), excessive thirst (polydipsia), and excessive hunger (polyphagia). [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h3)

question: What is the fasting plasma glucose (FPG) threshold used to help diagnose diabetes mellitus?

options.A: 70 mg/dL or higher
options.B: 100 mg/dL or higher
options.C: 126 mg/dL or higher
options.D: 200 mg/dL or higher

explanation: A fasting plasma glucose level of 126 mg/dL or higher is a standard criterion for diagnosing diabetes. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h4)

question: What does the Glycated Hemoglobin (HbA1c) test primarily measure?

options.A: Immediate blood sugar levels over the last hour
options.B: Long-term glycemic control over the preceding two to three months
options.C: Total cholesterol and lipid profiles
options.D: Renal filtration rate and urine output

explanation: The HbA1c test reflects average blood glucose levels over the past 2 to 3 months, offering a view of long-term control. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h4)

question: What is typically considered the first-line oral medication for managing Type 2 diabetes?

options.A: Metformin
options.B: Insulin glargine
options.C: Glibenclamide
options.D: Acarbose

explanation: Metformin, a biguanide, is the standard first-line oral hypoglycemic agent for Type 2 diabetes. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h5)

question: Why is proper injection site rotation important for patients receiving insulin therapy?

options.A: To prevent hypoglycemia at night
options.B: To prevent lipodystrophy and ensure consistent insulin absorption
options.C: To stimulate faster pancreatic insulin production
options.D: To reduce the cost of purchasing syringes

explanation: Rotating injection sites prevents skin damage and fatty lumps known as lipodystrophy, which can erraticize insulin absorption. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h5)

question: What is a recommended weekly amount of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise for individuals with diabetes?

options.A: 30 minutes total per week
options.B: At least 150 minutes per week
options.C: 5 hours per day
options.D: Exercise is not recommended for diabetics

explanation: Guidelines recommend at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic exercise weekly to improve insulin sensitivity. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h6)

question: How should dietary counseling be approached in the Nigerian healthcare setting?

options.A: By advising complete elimination of all local carbohydrates
options.B: By prescribing expensive imported meal options exclusively
options.C: By incorporating local food staples in balanced, portion-controlled meals
options.D: By letting patients eat whatever they desire without restrictions

explanation: Dietary advice should be culturally relevant, making use of local staples in balanced, healthy portions. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h6)

question: Which acute complication is characterized by severe hyperglycemia, dehydration, and ketoacidosis, typically seen in Type 1 diabetes?

options.A: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)
options.B: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS)
options.C: Hypoglycemic shock
options.D: Gestational hypertension

explanation: DKA features severe hyperglycemia, ketosis, and metabolic acidosis, and is most frequently seen in Type 1 diabetes. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h7)

question: What type of long-term complication does diabetic retinopathy represent?

options.A: Macrovascular complication
options.B: Acute metabolic crisis
options.C: Microvascular complication
options.D: Infectious complication

explanation: Diabetic retinopathy involves damage to small blood vessels in the eyes, classifying it as a microvascular complication. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h7)

question: What is a major benefit of establishing community-based diabetes support groups in primary health centers?

options.A: They completely cure Type 1 diabetes
options.B: They provide a platform for peer support, group education, and routine screening
options.C: They replace the need for any pharmacological treatment
options.D: They eliminate the cost of all medications

explanation: Support groups offer peer encouragement, shared learning, and routine check-ups in a community-friendly setting. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h8)

question: Why is patient education on daily foot care critical in diabetes management?

options.A: To prevent nail growth disorders
options.B: To catch peripheral neuropathy and prevent severe foot ulcers and amputations
options.C: To stimulate better insulin production in the feet
options.D: To cure visual impairment caused by retinopathy

explanation: Routine foot care helps detect early loss of sensation or injuries, preventing infections, ulcers, and subsequent amputations. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h8)

question: What does the systolic blood pressure reading represent?

options.A: The pressure in the arteries when the heart rests between beats
options.B: The pressure in the arteries when the heart beats
options.C: The average pressure in the veins over a 24-hour period
options.D: The resistance offered by peripheral capillaries

explanation: Systolic blood pressure represents the pressure exerted in the arteries when the heart contracts or beats. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h1)

question: What is the primary role of Primary Health Care (PHC) in government nutrition policies?

options.A: To serve as the main point for curative surgery
options.B: To act as the strategic level for executing nutritional interventions
options.C: To exclusively import foreign nutritional supplements
options.D: To replace agricultural sector responsibilities

explanation: PHC serves as the first point of contact and is the most strategic level for executing community-based nutritional interventions and health promotion. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T18#GNS214_U1_T18_h1)

question: Which vulnerable populations are particularly impacted by malnutrition according to public health principles?

options.A: Infants, pregnant women, and the elderly
options.B: Only adolescent males
options.C: Retired corporate executives
options.D: International tourists

explanation: Infants, pregnant women, and the elderly are among the most vulnerable groups experiencing high morbidity and mortality from malnutrition. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T18#GNS214_U1_T18_h1)

question: What is a primary objective of national food security and agricultural production policies?

options.A: To ensure citizens have access to sufficient, safe, and nutritious food
options.B: To completely eliminate the importation of all industrial goods
options.C: To shift the entire population away from farming
options.D: To focus exclusively on luxury food production

explanation: Food security policies aim to ensure physical, social, and economic access to sufficient, safe, and nutritious food for everyone. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T18#GNS214_U1_T18_h2)

question: How does chronic food insecurity directly impact children?

options.A: It enhances their cognitive abilities
options.B: It leads to stunting, wasting, and developmental impairments
options.C: It causes rapid weight gain
options.D: It has no measurable health impact

explanation: Chronic food insecurity leads to malnutrition manifestations like stunting and wasting, which permanently impair physical and cognitive development. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T18#GNS214_U1_T18_h2)

question: Why are temperature controls and sanitary conditions important in transport vehicles during food distribution?

options.A: To accelerate the ripening of non-food items
options.B: To inhibit microbial growth and prevent spoilage of perishable goods
options.C: To increase fuel efficiency
options.D: To lower the cost of vehicle maintenance

explanation: Proper temperature controls and hygiene inhibit microbial growth, protecting perishable goods like milk and meat from spoiling and causing foodborne illness. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T18#GNS214_U1_T18_h3)

question: What is a common consequence of disruptions in the food supply chain caused by poor infrastructure?

options.A: Abundant and free food supplies
options.B: Artificial scarcity and inflated food prices
options.C: Immediate eradication of malnutrition
options.D: Improved nutritional status nationwide

explanation: Poor infrastructure and distribution bottlenecks frequently result in artificial scarcity and hiked prices, reducing food accessibility for vulnerable populations. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T18#GNS214_U1_T18_h3)

question: What dangerous mycotoxins can proliferate when grains are stored improperly in damp conditions?

options.A: Penicillin variants
options.B: Aflatoxins produced by molds like Aspergillus
options.C: Insulin-based toxins
options.D: Botulinum neurotoxins

explanation: Improper storage encourages mold growth such as Aspergillus species, which produce harmful aflatoxins linked to liver damage and cancer. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T18#GNS214_U1_T18_h4)

question: What is a major benefit of reducing post-harvest losses in Nigeria?

options.A: Increasing available food supplies without needing more farmland
options.B: Increasing the cost of agricultural machinery
options.C: Eliminating the need for food transportation
options.D: Promoting the export of spoiled foods

explanation: Minimizing post-harvest waste ensures more food reaches consumers, effectively boosting available food supplies without requiring additional agricultural land. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T18#GNS214_U1_T18_h4)

question: Which agencies are primarily responsible for enforcing food safety regulations and quality control in Nigeria?

options.A: NAFDAC and SON
options.B: Ministry of Interior and Police Force
options.C: Central Bank and Federal Inland Revenue
options.D: National Youth Service Corps

explanation: Agencies like NAFDAC and SON are mandated to regulate and enforce quality control standards for food, drugs, and other consumables in Nigeria. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T18#GNS214_U1_T18_h5)

question: Why are food labeling laws regarding expiration dates and ingredients important for consumers?

options.A: They help manufacturers increase product prices
options.B: They empower consumers and patients to make informed, safe dietary choices
options.C: They simplify the transport logistics of food items
options.D: They eliminate the need for agricultural subsidies

explanation: Clear labeling of expiration dates and ingredients gives consumers the necessary information to choose safe, unexpired foods. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T18#GNS214_U1_T18_h5)

question: What tool is commonly used by PHC workers during clinical assessments to measure nutritional status in children?

options.A: Sphygmomanometer
options.B: Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) tape
options.C: Stethoscope
options.D: Ophthalmoscope

explanation: MUAC tapes and growth charts are standard anthropometric tools used by nurses and PHC workers to screen for malnutrition in community settings. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T18#GNS214_U1_T18_h6)

question: Which infant feeding practice is heavily promoted by PHC workers during community health education sessions?

options.A: Early introduction of solid foods at two weeks
options.B: Exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of life
options.C: Cow's milk feeding from birth
options.D: Complete avoidance of breast milk

explanation: PHC workers actively promote exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months of life as a core policy-backed nutritional intervention. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T18#GNS214_U1_T18_h6)

question: What is a major environmental factor currently challenging agricultural production and food security in Nigeria?

options.A: Excessive and predictable seasonal snowfalls
options.B: Climate change causing unpredictable rainfall and droughts
options.C: Rising sea levels in desert regions
options.D: Constant year-round temperate weather

explanation: Climate change resulting in unpredictable rainfall and prolonged droughts severely threatens agricultural yields and overall food security. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T18#GNS214_U1_T18_h7)

question: What is required as part of the future directions for Nigerian food policy to overcome current obstacles?

options.A: Complete reliance on food importation
options.B: An integrated approach including climate-smart agriculture and digital supply tracking
options.C: Reduction of primary health care funding
options.D: Elimination of all food safety regulations

explanation: Overcoming current policy challenges requires integrated solutions such as climate-smart farming, digital tracking, and better inter-ministerial coordination. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T18#GNS214_U1_T18_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of conducting nutritional assessments in primary health care?

options.A: To diagnose rare genetic disorders
options.B: To identify nutritional deficiencies, excesses, or risks early
options.C: To prescribe pharmaceutical supplements without evaluation
options.D: To replace standard medical examinations

explanation: Nutritional assessments are primarily used to identify deficiencies, excesses, or risks of malnutrition early so that targeted interventions can be applied. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T19#GNS214_U1_T19_h1)

question: Which of the following represents the standard framework domains of nutritional assessment?

options.A: ABCD method
options.B: XYZ protocol
options.C: Vitals and Labs approach
options.D: Physical fitness matrix

explanation: The evaluation process typically follows the ABCD method, which stands for Anthropometric, Biochemical, Clinical, and Dietary evaluations. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T19#GNS214_U1_T19_h1)

question: Which anthropometric tool is most commonly used in community settings to rapidly screen children for acute malnutrition?

options.A: Sphygmomanometer
options.B: Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC) tape
options.C: Glucometer
options.D: Stethoscope

explanation: MUAC is vital for rapidly screening young children for acute malnutrition using color-coded tapes in community settings. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T19#GNS214_U1_T19_h2)

question: Why is proper technique and equipment calibration important in anthropometric measurements?

options.A: To prevent clinical misclassification of nutritional status
options.B: To reduce the cost of medical supplies
options.C: To eliminate the need for dietary histories
options.D: To diagnose infectious diseases quickly

explanation: Accurate techniques and calibrated tools prevent errors that could lead to the misclassification of a patient's nutritional status. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T19#GNS214_U1_T19_h2)

question: Which body tissues typically manifest signs of nutritional deficiencies earliest due to rapid cell turnover?

options.A: Bones and cartilage
options.B: Skin, hair, eyes, and nails
options.C: Deep skeletal muscles
options.D: Ligaments and tendons

explanation: Tissues with rapid cell turnover, such as the skin, hair, eyes, and nails, show physical signs of nutritional distress earliest. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T19#GNS214_U1_T19_h3)

question: What key physical sign is commonly associated with severe iron deficiency anemia during a clinical exam?

options.A: Bitot's spots
options.B: Pallor of the conjunctiva and nail beds
options.C: Edema of the lower extremities
options.D: Sparse, depigmented hair

explanation: Iron deficiency frequently presents with pallor of the conjunctiva and nail beds due to reduced hemoglobin levels. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T19#GNS214_U1_T19_h3)

question: Which tool is commonly used to evaluate a patient's food intake over the past day?

options.A: 24-hour dietary recall
options.B: Mid-upper arm circumference measurement
options.C: Complete blood count
options.D: Urinalysis dipstick

explanation: A 24-hour dietary recall is a standard method used to collect data on everything an individual consumed over the preceding 24 hours. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T19#GNS214_U1_T19_h4)

question: What are the four core dimensions of food security examined during a family assessment?

options.A: Production, distribution, cooking, and storage
options.B: Availability, accessibility, utilization, and stability
options.C: Cost, marketing, packaging, and consumption
options.D: Importation, taxation, processing, and sale

explanation: Food security is evaluated based on its four core dimensions: availability, accessibility, utilization, and stability. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T19#GNS214_U1_T19_h4)

question: Which laboratory test is most commonly used to screen for anemia in clinical practice?

options.A: Serum retinol assay
options.B: Hemoglobin and packed cell volume (PCV)
options.C: Urinalysis culture
options.D: Fasting blood glucose test

explanation: Hemoglobin and PCV are standard laboratory tests used to screen patients for anemia. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T19#GNS214_U1_T19_h5)

question: What non-nutritional factor can significantly alter biochemical markers such as serum proteins and iron levels?

options.A: Acute or chronic inflammation and infection
options.B: High physical activity levels
options.C: Consuming water before the test
options.D: Time of day the sample was collected

explanation: Inflammation and infections trigger acute-phase responses that can alter biochemical markers, making interpretation complex. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T19#GNS214_U1_T19_h5)

question: Why are infants and young children considered a highly vulnerable group for malnutrition?

options.A: They consume too many calories naturally
options.B: They have high nutritional requirements relative to body size for rapid growth
options.C: They are immune to infectious diseases
options.D: They have fully developed digestive systems

explanation: Infants and young children have high nutrient needs for rapid growth and development, making them especially vulnerable to nutritional deficits. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T19#GNS214_U1_T19_h6)

question: What physiological state increases a woman's demand for iron, folic acid, and protein?

options.A: Menopause
options.B: Pregnancy and lactation
options.C: Adolescent growth cessation
options.D: Advanced aging

explanation: Pregnancy and lactation significantly increase a woman's physiological demand for key nutrients to support the fetus and milk production. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T19#GNS214_U1_T19_h6)

question: What is recommended duration for exclusive breastfeeding according to optimal infant nutrition guidelines?

options.A: First three months of life
options.B: First six months of life
options.C: First twelve months of life
options.D: Until the child can walk

explanation: Exclusive breastfeeding is recommended for the first six months of life to provide ideal nutrition and immune protection. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T19#GNS214_U1_T19_h7)

question: Which educational approach is most effective when teaching mothers how to prepare local complementary foods?

options.A: Handing out complex medical textbooks
options.B: Demonstration and Re-demonstration method
options.C: Giving strict instructions without explanation
options.D: Requiring a written examination

explanation: The demonstration and re-demonstration method ensures that mothers fully understand and can correctly replicate food preparation techniques. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T19#GNS214_U1_T19_h7)

question: What does the 'E' stand for in the acronym IEC within public health?

options.A: Education
options.B: Environment
options.C: Evaluation
options.D: Emergency

explanation: In public health communication frameworks, IEC stands for Information, Education, and Communication. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T2#GNS214_U1_T2_h1)

question: Why is IEC considered a core component of primary health care rather than just clinical treatment?

options.A: It empowers communities to adopt preventive habits before illness occurs
options.B: It completely replaces the need for doctors and hospitals in rural areas
options.C: It provides immediate surgical interventions for trauma patients
options.D: It focuses exclusively on generating revenue for health facilities

explanation: IEC focuses on proactive health promotion and disease prevention rather than reactive curative care alone. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T2#GNS214_U1_T2_h1)

question: Which health model posits that individuals take action based on perceived susceptibility, severity, benefits, and barriers?

options.A: General Adaptation Syndrome
options.B: Epidemiological Triad
options.C: Biomedical Germ Theory
options.D: Health Belief Model
