options.B: An exclusive hospital-based isolation protocol
options.C: Strict commercial trade embargoes on food products
options.D: Complete eradication of all wildlife populations

question: What is epidemiological surveillance primarily defined as in a healthcare setting?

options.A: The physical quarantine of an entire city during an outbreak
options.B: The ongoing, systematic collection, analysis, and interpretation of health data
options.C: The immediate prescription of broad-spectrum antibiotics to all patients
options.D: The laboratory synthesis of new vaccines

explanation: Surveillance involves the systematic collection, analysis, and interpretation of health data to monitor disease trends and detect outbreaks early. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T80#GNS214_U1_T80_h5)

question: Why are Primary Health Care (PHC) facilities vital for reservoir identification in Nigeria?

options.A: They possess advanced genetic sequencing laboratories on every ward

options.C: They are exclusively responsible for international travel clearances
options.D: They prevent patients from interacting with animals

question: What is the primary management approach when dealing with human reservoirs of infection?

options.A: Culling and mass destruction of personal property
options.B: Prompt diagnosis, effective antimicrobial treatment, and isolation or quarantine
options.C: Pest extermination and rodent-proofing buildings
options.D: Boiling local soil and vegetation

explanation: Human reservoirs are managed through prompt diagnosis, curative treatment, and appropriate isolation or quarantine to prevent further spread. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T80#GNS214_U1_T80_h6)

question: Which of the following interventions specifically targets environmental reservoirs?

options.A: Administering antibiotics to infected patients
options.B: Vaccinating domestic dogs
options.C: Water purification and proper sewage disposal
options.D: Contact tracing of human travelers

explanation: Environmental reservoirs like water and soil are managed through sanitation improvements such as water purification and proper waste disposal. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T80#GNS214_U1_T80_h6)

question: How do nurses prevent the spread of infections from human reservoirs within hospital wards?

options.A: By implementing rigorous standard and transmission-based precautions
options.B: By permanently closing hospital facilities during outbreaks
options.C: By outsourcing all patient care to veterinary specialists
options.D: By avoiding physical contact with all patients

explanation: Nurses use standard and transmission-based precautions (like PPE and hand hygiene) to stop nosocomial transmission from human reservoirs in hospitals. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T80#GNS214_U1_T80_h7)

question: What is a key community-level duty of a nurse in reservoir-focused disease prevention?

options.A: Enforcing quarantine through military intervention
options.B: Educating families on safe food storage and personal hygiene
options.C: Manufacturing pharmaceuticals in primary health centers
options.D: Destroying all local animal populations proactively

explanation: Nurses educate communities on preventive practices like safe food storage, handwashing, and hygiene to mitigate environmental and zoonotic risks. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T80#GNS214_U1_T80_h7)

question: What is the primary definition of the route of transmission in the context of infectious diseases?

options.A: The genetic makeup of an infectious agent
options.B: The specific mechanism by which a pathogen moves from a source to a susceptible host
options.C: The time it takes for symptoms to appear after exposure
options.D: The rate at which a disease spreads through a population

explanation: The route of transmission refers to the specific mechanism or pathway by which a pathogen travels from its reservoir or source to a susceptible host. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T81#GNS214_U1_T81_h1)

question: Why is understanding transmission routes particularly important for nursing students in clinical practice?

options.A: To diagnose patients without needing laboratory tests
options.B: To implement targeted interventions and infection prevention control measures
options.C: To prescribe appropriate antibiotic therapy independently
options.D: To calculate the exact mortality rate of an outbreak

explanation: Knowing how pathogens travel allows nurses to apply appropriate standard and transmission-based precautions to break the cycle of infection. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T81#GNS214_U1_T81_h1)

question: Which of the following components make up the Epidemiological Triangle?

options.A: Agent, Host, and Environment
options.B: Reservoir, Portal of Exit, and Portal of Entry
options.C: Infectious Agent, Transmission, and Susceptible Host
options.D: Bacteria, Virus, and Parasite

explanation: The Epidemiological Triangle is composed of the agent, the host, and the environment, which interact to cause disease. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T81#GNS214_U1_T81_h2)

question: How can a nurse effectively stop an infection using the Chain of Infection concept?

options.A: By waiting until the host develops immunity
options.B: By breaking any single link in the six-step chain
options.C: By strengthening the infectious agent
options.D: By expanding the reservoir of the pathogen

explanation: An infection requires all links of the chain to be intact; therefore, breaking even a single link halts the transmission process. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T81#GNS214_U1_T81_h2)

question: What defines direct contact transmission?

options.A: The transfer of pathogens through contaminated food or water
options.B: The inhalation of droplets suspended in the air
options.C: The physical transfer of microorganisms through body surface-to-body surface contact
options.D: The transmission of disease via insect vectors like mosquitoes

explanation: Direct contact transmission involves the physical transfer of microorganisms through direct body surface-to-body surface contact between an infected person and a susceptible host. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T81#GNS214_U1_T81_h3)

question: Which of the following is a primary nursing intervention to prevent direct contact transmission in clinical settings?

options.A: Administering prophylactic antibiotics to all visitors
options.B: Wearing appropriate gloves and performing rigorous hand hygiene
options.C: Placing patients in negative pressure isolation rooms for all admissions
options.D: Restricting all nutritional intake for hospitalized clients

explanation: Rigorous hand hygiene and the proper use of gloves are essential standard precautions that prevent the direct transfer of pathogens from hands to patients. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T81#GNS214_U1_T81_h3)

question: What is a fomite in the context of indirect contact transmission?

options.A: A living insect that carries a pathogen
options.B: An inanimate object contaminated with infectious microorganisms
options.C: A microscopic droplet suspended in the air
options.D: An infected animal reservoir

explanation: A fomite is an inanimate object, such as a stethoscope or door handle, that can harbor and transfer infectious agents to a susceptible host. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T81#GNS214_U1_T81_h4)

question: Which nursing action is most effective in preventing indirect contact transmission via fomites?

options.A: Performing hand hygiene between every patient contact and disinfecting equipment
options.B: Replacing all hospital furniture daily
options.C: Isolating all patients in single rooms regardless of diagnosis
options.D: Avoiding the use of any metal instruments in clinical practice

explanation: Hand hygiene and proper equipment disinfection prevent pathogens from being transferred from inanimate objects or previous patients to new hosts. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T81#GNS214_U1_T81_h4)

question: What is a key characteristic that distinguishes droplet transmission from airborne transmission?

options.A: Droplet particles travel long distances on air currents.
options.B: Droplet particles are heavy, travel short distances (usually under one meter), and do not remain suspended long.
options.C: Airborne transmission only occurs through direct physical touch.
options.D: Airborne pathogens cannot infect human respiratory tracts.

explanation: Droplet particles are relatively heavy and travel short distances (typically under a meter), whereas airborne particles remain suspended and travel further. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T81#GNS214_U1_T81_h5)

question: Which protective measure is specifically required when caring for a patient with suspected pulmonary tuberculosis (an airborne infection)?

options.A: Surgical gloves only
options.B: A standard surgical mask
options.C: A fitted N95 respirator mask and proper ventilation
options.D: A plastic face shield without respiratory protection

explanation: Airborne precautions for diseases like tuberculosis require fitted particulate respirators (like N95 masks) and adequate room ventilation to protect against inhaled droplet nuclei. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T81#GNS214_U1_T81_h5)

question: What defines zoonotic transmission of infectious diseases?

options.A: Transmission of pathogens strictly between human beings via fomites
options.B: Infections that naturally pass from vertebrate animals to humans
options.C: The spread of disease solely through airborne dust particles
options.D: Infections acquired exclusively inside operating theaters

explanation: Zoonotic transmission occurs when pathogens are naturally transmitted from vertebrate animals to humans through contact, bites, or contaminated products. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T81#GNS214_U1_T81_h6)

question: Which of the following is a primary vector-borne disease prevalent in Nigeria that nurses frequently encounter?

options.A: Malaria
options.B: Tuberculosis
options.C: Tetanus
options.D: Cholera

explanation: Malaria is a classic vector-borne disease transmitted by infected female Anopheles mosquitoes, posing a major public health challenge in Nigeria. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T81#GNS214_U1_T81_h6)

question: What characterizes common vehicle transmission of infectious diseases?

options.A: A single contaminated source like food, water, or blood infects multiple individuals simultaneously.
options.B: Pathogens are transmitted exclusively through close personal kisses.
options.C: Infections are spread only by airborne respiratory droplets.
options.D: Diseases are passed strictly from mothers to their unborn infants.

explanation: Common vehicle transmission involves a single contaminated medium, such as water, food, or blood, that spreads an agent to many hosts, often causing outbreaks. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T81#GNS214_U1_T81_h7)

question: Which nursing practice is crucial for preventing bloodborne common vehicle transmission in a clinical setting?

options.A: Boiling all drinking water before patient consumption
options.B: Practicing safe injection techniques and proper handling of sharps
options.C: Isolating all patients who have respiratory infections
options.D: Ensuring routine use of insecticide-treated bed nets

explanation: Safe injection practices and careful handling of sharps prevent the transmission of bloodborne pathogens like HIV and Hepatitis B. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T81#GNS214_U1_T81_h7)

question: What is the primary focus of Primary Health Care (PHC) strategies regarding infectious diseases?

options.A: Constructing high-tech tertiary care surgical centers
options.B: Preventing disease transmission at the grassroots level through education and community participation
options.C: Importing expensive foreign medications for hospital pharmacies
options.D: Isolating infected patients permanently from society

explanation: PHC focuses on community-based preventative services, health education, and sanitation to stop disease transmission before it occurs. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T81#GNS214_U1_T81_h8)

question: How do routine immunization programs function as a primary health care strategy to interrupt transmission?

options.A: By curing patients who are already experiencing acute symptoms
options.B: By building community herd immunity against vaccine-preventable diseases
options.C: By eliminating insect vectors from the environment
options.D: By sterilizing all medical equipment in community clinics

explanation: Immunization builds herd immunity within a population, making it difficult for pathogens to find susceptible hosts and thus blocking transmission. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T81#GNS214_U1_T81_h8)

question: What term describes the natural habitat where an infectious agent typically lives, grows, and multiplies?

options.A: Carrier
options.B: Vector
options.C: Fomite
options.D: Reservoir

explanation: A reservoir is the ecological niche or natural habitat where a pathogen persists and reproduces over time. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T82#GNS214_U1_T82_h1)

question: How does a source of infection differ from a reservoir in epidemiological terms?

options.A: There is no functional difference; the two terms are interchangeable in clinical documentation.
options.B: The source refers only to viral pathogens, while the reservoir refers exclusively to bacterial agents.
options.C: The reservoir is always an animate object, whereas the source is strictly an inanimate surface.
options.D: The source is the immediate origin from which the pathogen passes to the host, whereas the reservoir is its long-term natural habitat.

explanation: While a reservoir maintains the pathogen in nature, the source is the specific entity that transfers it directly to a susceptible individual. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T82#GNS214_U1_T82_h1)

question: Which type of human source harbors and sheds a pathogen without ever developing clinical signs of illness?

options.A: Healthy carrier
options.B: Symptomatic patient
options.C: Convalescent case
options.D: Clinical case

explanation: A healthy carrier is infected and capable of transmitting the agent to others while remaining completely asymptomatic themselves. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T82#GNS214_U1_T82_h2)

question: A patient recovering from typhoid fever continues to excrete *Salmonella typhi* in their stool three months after all symptoms have vanished. How is this individual classified?

options.A: Convalescent carrier
options.B: Chronic carrier
options.C: Active clinical case
options.D: Healthy carrier

explanation: Shedding a pathogen long after recovery (often defined as exceeding several months or a year) categorizes a person as a chronic carrier. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T82#GNS214_U1_T82_h2)

question: What is the term for infectious diseases that are naturally transmissible from vertebrate animals to humans?

options.A: Saprophytic diseases
options.B: Zoonoses
options.C: Opportunistic mycoses
options.D: Nosocomial infections

explanation: Zoonoses are infections shared between animals and humans, such as rabies and anthrax. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T82#GNS214_U1_T82_h3)

question: A farmer presents with a severe skin infection and necrosis after handling damp soil contaminated with animal waste. What type of infection source is primarily responsible?

options.A: Endogenous microflora source
options.B: Environmental and soil source
options.C: Nosocomial fomite source
options.D: Strict human carrier source

explanation: Soil acts as an environmental reservoir and source for spore-forming pathogens like tetanus or anthrax. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T82#GNS214_U1_T82_h3)

question: Which mode of transmission involves an inanimate object, such as a contaminated stethoscope or bed rail, transferring a pathogen?

options.A: Fomite transmission
options.B: Direct droplet spread
options.C: Airborne droplet nuclei
options.D: Vector-borne transmission

explanation: Fomites are inanimate objects that can become contaminated with infectious agents and transfer them to new hosts. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T82#GNS214_U1_T82_h4)

question: An outbreak of malaria in a community is linked to stagnant water breeding mosquitoes. Which category of transmission does this represent?

options.A: Airborne droplet transmission
options.B: Vector-borne transmission
options.C: Fomite-mediated transmission
options.D: Direct contact transmission

explanation: Mosquitoes act as living vectors that transmit parasites like plasmodium from one host to another. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T82#GNS214_U1_T82_h4)

question: Why is early identification of an infection source critical in a hospital ward?

options.A: It halts further transmission by allowing targeted containment measures like isolation or equipment decontamination.
options.B: It eliminates the need for any subsequent hand hygiene protocols among the nursing staff.
options.C: it instantly cures patients who are already displaying severe symptoms of the disease.
options.D: It removes all environmental microorganisms from the entire hospital facility permanently.

explanation: Finding the source allows nurses and infection control teams to interrupt the transmission chain at its origin. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T82#GNS214_U1_T82_h5)

question: Which of the following is NOT a standard nursing intervention used to eliminate or control an infection source in a healthcare facility?

options.A: Isolating patients with active infectious diseases
options.B: Ignoring positive culture results to avoid paperwork
options.C: Properly disposing of biohazardous waste
options.D: Enforcing rigorous equipment sterilization protocols

explanation: Ignoring diagnostic results actively undermines infection control and endangers patient safety; all other options are valid containment strategies. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T82#GNS214_U1_T82_h5)

question: What is the primary physiological function of the immune system?

options.A: To regulate blood pressure and cardiac output
options.B: To recognize and protect the body against harmful pathogens and foreign substances
options.C: To produce red blood cells for oxygen transport
options.D: To digest nutrients in the gastrointestinal tract

explanation: The immune system is specifically designed to recognize and defend the body against foreign invaders, toxins, and abnormal cells. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T83#GNS214_U1_T83_h1)

question: What term describes the immune system's ability to recognize the body's own tissues as 'self' and avoid attacking them?

options.A: Hypersensitivity
options.B: Immunocompetence
options.C: Self-tolerance
options.D: Seroconversion

explanation: Self-tolerance allows the immune system to differentiate between healthy body cells ('self') and harmful agents ('non-self'). [learn more](GNS214_U1_T83#GNS214_U1_T83_h1)

question: Which characteristic is unique to innate immunity compared to adaptive immunity?

options.A: It provides highly specific responses to single pathogens
options.B: It requires weeks to activate upon initial exposure
options.C: It is present from birth and provides non-specific protection
options.D: It generates long-lasting immunological memory

explanation: Innate immunity is present from birth and acts rapidly in a non-specific manner without creating long-term memory. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T83#GNS214_U1_T83_h2)

question: Which cells are primarily responsible for the adaptive immune response?

options.A: Red blood cells and platelets
options.B: Epithelial cells and keratinocytes
options.C: T lymphocytes and B lymphocytes
options.D: Fibroblasts and osteocytes

explanation: T cells and B cells are lymphocytes that drive the specific, memory-forming adaptive immune response. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T83#GNS214_U1_T83_h2)

question: What is a defining characteristic of active immunity?

options.A: It provides immediate protection that fades quickly
options.B: It relies entirely on maternal antibodies passed via breast milk
options.C: It stimulates the body's own cells to produce antibodies and memory cells
options.D: It involves injecting preformed antitoxins for immediate treatment

explanation: Active immunity involves the individual's own immune system actively responding to antigens to form antibodies and long-lasting memory. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T83#GNS214_U1_T83_h3)

question: How do infants acquire natural passive immunity from their mothers?

options.A: Through routine childhood immunizations at primary health centers
options.B: Through placental transfer of IgG and ingestion of colostrum
options.C: By contracting mild childhood infections naturally
options.D: Through the administration of intravenous immunoglobulin

explanation: Maternal antibodies are transferred naturally across the placenta and through breast milk, providing temporary passive protection to newborns. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T83#GNS214_U1_T83_h3)

question: Which of the following describes artificial active immunity?

options.A: Receiving breast milk from an immune mother
options.B: Recovering from a natural bout of measles
options.C: Receiving a vaccination to stimulate antibody production
options.D: Receiving an injection of antivenom following a snakebite

explanation: Vaccination is an artificial method used to actively stimulate the individual's immune system to produce protective antibodies. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T83#GNS214_U1_T83_h4)

question: What is the primary purpose of artificial passive immunity in clinical practice?

options.A: To provide lifelong immunity against viral mutations
options.B: To stimulate the bone marrow to produce new lymphocytes
options.C: To provide immediate, short-term protection via preformed antibodies
options.D: To replace active cellular immunity in immunodeficient patients

explanation: Artificial passive immunity delivers ready-made antibodies for immediate protection against acute toxins or infections. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T83#GNS214_U1_T83_h4)

question: What is an antigen?

options.A: A Y-shaped protein produced by plasma cells
options.B: A foreign substance that triggers an immune response
options.C: An enzyme that breaks down bacterial cell walls
options.D: A hormone regulating white blood cell production

explanation: An antigen is any foreign molecule or toxin that the immune system recognizes and targets for an immune response. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T83#GNS214_U1_T83_h5)

question: Which cells are responsible for secreting antibodies during an adaptive immune response?

options.A: Cytotoxic T cells
options.B: Natural killer cells
options.C: Plasma cells
options.D: Erythrocytes

explanation: B lymphocytes differentiate into plasma cells, which are the specialized factories that produce and secrete antibodies. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T83#GNS214_U1_T83_h5)

question: What is the primary benefit of herd immunity for vulnerable populations?

options.A: It guarantees that they will never develop allergies
options.B: It provides indirect protection by interrupting the chain of infection
options.C: It permanently alters their genetic susceptibility to pathogens
options.D: It replaces the need for innate physical barriers

explanation: Herd immunity interrupts disease transmission, offering indirect protection to individuals who cannot be vaccinated. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T83#GNS214_U1_T83_h6)

question: How is community herd immunity typically achieved in public health programs?

options.A: Through widespread antibiotic prophylaxis
options.B: By ensuring high vaccination coverage within the population
options.C: Through mandatory quarantine of all infected individuals
options.D: By improving urban sanitation and waste management alone

explanation: High vaccination coverage is the primary and safest method used to establish community herd immunity. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T83#GNS214_U1_T83_h6)

question: How does severe malnutrition affect the human immune response?

options.A: It enhances white blood cell production and function
options.B: It impairs immune cell proliferation and antibody production
options.C: It permanently cures autoimmune diseases
options.D: It accelerates the rate of immunosenescence

explanation: Malnutrition starves the body of essential nutrients needed for immune cell development and antibody synthesis, weakening defenses. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T83#GNS214_U1_T83_h7)

question: What term describes the gradual deterioration of immune function associated with advancing age?

options.A: Immunosenescence
options.B: Seroconversion
options.C: Hypersensitivity
options.D: Autoimmunity

explanation: Immunosenescence refers to the natural decline in immune system efficiency that occurs as people grow older. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T83#GNS214_U1_T83_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of epidemiology in primary health care settings?

options.A: To manufacture pharmaceutical drugs for local clinics
options.B: To study the distribution and patterns of health conditions and diseases
options.C: To handle administrative hospital budgeting and financing
options.D: To replace the role of clinical physicians in diagnosing patients

explanation: Epidemiology provides the scientific framework used to study the distribution, patterns, and determinants of health conditions and diseases in defined populations. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T84#GNS214_U1_T84_h1)

question: How does mastering core epidemiological terms help community health nurses in Nigeria?

options.A: It enables them to effectively track disease trends and allocate resources efficiently
options.B: It allows them to bypass the need for community health education
options.C: It guarantees complete eradication of all diseases within a week
options.D: It stops patients from visiting traditional healers

explanation: Knowing these terms allows healthcare workers to communicate effectively, track disease trends accurately, and allocate limited medical resources efficiently to communities in need. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T84#GNS214_U1_T84_h1)

question: Which of the following best defines the incubation period?

options.A: The time between symptom onset and full recovery
options.B: The duration of time a patient spends admitted in a hospital ward
options.C: The time interval between initial exposure to an infectious agent and the appearance of first symptoms
options.D: The period when a patient develops permanent immunity to a pathogen

explanation: The incubation period is specifically defined as the time interval between the initial exposure to an infectious agent and the appearance of the first clinical signs or symptoms of the disease. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T84#GNS214_U1_T84_h2)

question: What typically characterizes a patient who is currently in the incubation period of an infection?

options.A: They experience severe, life-threatening symptoms immediately
options.B: They have not yet developed noticeable clinical signs or symptoms of the illness
options.C: They are completely immune and cannot develop the disease
options.D: They always require immediate surgical intervention

explanation: During the incubation interval, an individual typically does not experience noticeable illness and shows no clinical signs or symptoms yet. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T84#GNS214_U1_T84_h2)

question: What event primarily triggers the appearance of clinical symptoms after the incubation period?

options.A: The complete destruction of the pathogen by initial skin barriers
options.B: Tissue damage, toxin accumulation, or inflammatory responses reaching a critical threshold
options.C: The immediate drop in the patient's body temperature below normal
options.D: The cessation of all cellular replication within the host

explanation: Symptoms emerge when the cumulative tissue damage, toxin accumulation, or the host's robust inflammatory cytokine response reaches a critical threshold that disrupts normal physiological functioning. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T84#GNS214_U1_T84_h3)

question: Why are clinical symptoms absent during the early stages of the incubation period?

options.A: Pathogen numbers are initially low and immune responses are still developing
options.B: The pathogen is completely dormant and never replicates
options.C: Human cells actively block all infectious agents permanently
options.D: Antibiotics are automatically produced by the liver during this time

explanation: Because pathogen numbers are initially low and immune responses are still ramping up, overt clinical symptoms remain absent during this phase. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T84#GNS214_U1_T84_h3)

question: How does a higher infectious dose generally affect the length of an incubation period?

options.A: It extends the incubation period by several months
options.B: It has no impact whatsoever on the disease timeline
options.C: It often results in a shorter incubation period
options.D: It completely prevents any symptoms from ever appearing

explanation: A higher number of invading pathogens entering the body often results in a shorter incubation period because it takes less time for the microorganism to reach critical mass. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T84#GNS214_U1_T84_h4)

question: Which of the following host factors can influence the duration of an incubation period?

options.A: Nutritional status and immune competence
options.B: The brand of soap used for handwashing
options.C: The patient's favorite recreational activities
options.D: The architectural design of the local health clinic

explanation: Host-related factors such as age, nutritional status, genetic predisposition, underlying chronic illnesses, and overall immune competence heavily impact the incubation phase. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T84#GNS214_U1_T84_h4)

question: Why is taking a detailed exposure and travel history important when assessing a patient?

options.A: It allows the nurse to calculate timelines and narrow down differential diagnoses
options.B: It replaces the need for laboratory blood investigations entirely
options.C: It determines how much the patient will be billed for hospital care
options.D: It ensures the patient receives immediate surgical clearance

explanation: Taking a detailed exposure history allows the nurse to calculate backwards and narrow down the differential diagnosis to specific pathogens matching that incubation window. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T84#GNS214_U1_T84_h5)

question: If a patient develops severe symptoms within a few hours of eating contaminated food, what does the short interval suggest to a nurse?

options.A: A viral infection with a very long incubation period
options.B: A bacterial toxin-mediated food poisoning rather than a slower-developing infection
options.C: That the patient has been infected for several weeks
options.D: That no infectious agent is involved in the illness

explanation: Rapid symptom onset points toward pre-formed bacterial toxins (like staphylococcal intoxication) rather than infections that require prolonged replication time. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T84#GNS214_U1_T84_h5)

question: How is the duration of quarantine determined for individuals exposed to a contagious disease?

options.A: It is always set to a standard flat rate of exactly three days
options.B: It is matched to the maximum known incubation period of the specific pathogen
options.C: It lasts until the patient fully recovers from all symptoms
options.D: It depends entirely on the patient's personal preference

explanation: The duration of quarantine is purposefully matched to the maximum known incubation period of the specific pathogen to ensure exposed individuals do not develop illness later. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T84#GNS214_U1_T84_h6)

question: What is the primary goal of public health contact tracing during an infectious disease outbreak?

options.A: To collect financial donations for hospital equipment
options.B: To identify exposed individuals, monitor them, and cut chains of transmission
options.C: To enforce mandatory vaccination for the entire global population
options.D: To replace standard hospital nursing care documentation

explanation: Contact tracing involves identifying, assessing, and managing exposed individuals to monitor symptoms and cut transmission chains early. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T84#GNS214_U1_T84_h6)

question: How do public health surveillance systems use the incubation period during an outbreak?

options.A: To calculate generation times and predict how fast the outbreak will spread
options.B: To determine the exact financial cost of hospital building repairs
options.C: To schedule routine staff leave for nurses and doctors
options.D: To calculate the daily dietary needs of hospitalized patients

explanation: Surveillance systems use the incubation period to calculate generation times and predict how fast an outbreak will spread through a population. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T84#GNS214_U1_T84_h7)

question: What is the purpose of interventions like ring vaccination during an outbreak?

options.A: To decorate public health clinics for awareness campaigns
options.B: To confer immunity to contacts within a specific incubation window before disease strikes
options.C: To cure patients who are already in the advanced stages of illness
options.D: To disinfect water supplies in urban communities

explanation: Ring vaccination strategies depend on vaccinating contacts within a specific window of the incubation period to confer immunity before the pathogen can cause clinical disease. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T84#GNS214_U1_T84_h7)

question: Which epidemiological term measures the frequency of new cases of a disease within a specific time period in a population at risk?

options.A: Prevalence
options.B: Incidence
options.C: Morbidity
options.D: Mortality

explanation: Incidence specifically measures the frequency of newly occurring cases within a defined timeframe, which helps nurses determine the speed of transmission. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T85#GNS214_U1_T85_h1)

question: What does the term prevalence represent in community health data?

options.A: The total number of deaths in a population
options.B: The total number of new cases only
options.C: The total number of existing cases, both old and new, at a given time
options.D: The rate of physical or mental well-being departure

explanation: Prevalence quantifies all existing cases at a specific point in time, reflecting the overall disease burden in the community. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T85#GNS214_U1_T85_h1)

question: How is a disease outbreak best defined in public health practice?

options.A: A single isolated case of a rare disease
options.B: The total eradication of a communicable infection
options.C: The occurrence of more cases of a disease than expected in a given area and time
options.D: The normal baseline presence of an endemic illness in a community

explanation: An outbreak is identified when disease frequency exceeds the expected baseline for a specific area and time frame. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T85#GNS214_U1_T85_h2)

question: Who is the primary local contact person that community health nurses should notify upon suspecting an outbreak in a Nigerian LGA?

options.A: The Disease Surveillance and Notification Officer (DSNO)
options.B: The Minister of Finance
options.C: The Chief Medical Director of a private hospital abroad
options.D: The local market association president

explanation: Suspected outbreaks must be reported promptly to the LGA Disease Surveillance and Notification Officer (DSNO) to initiate a coordinated public health response. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T85#GNS214_U1_T85_h2)

question: Which term describes a disease that is constantly present at a steady, predictable baseline frequency within a specific geographic region?

options.A: Pandemic
options.B: Epidemic
options.C: Endemic
options.D: Outbreak

explanation: An endemic disease maintains a constant, expected baseline presence in a specific geographic area over time. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T85#GNS214_U1_T85_h3)

question: What distinguishes a pandemic from an epidemic or outbreak?

options.A: It only affects children under five years old.
options.B: It has spread across multiple countries or continents globally.
options.C: It is restricted to a single village or LGA.
options.D: It has a 100% mortality rate.

explanation: A pandemic is an epidemic that crosses international borders, affecting multiple countries and continents worldwide. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T85#GNS214_U1_T85_h3)

question: Which pathogen is primarily responsible for waterborne cholera outbreaks during periods of poor sanitation or heavy rainfall?

options.A: Plasmodium falciparum
options.B: Vibrio cholerae
options.C: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
options.D: Lassa virus

explanation: Vibrio cholerae is the bacterium responsible for acute watery diarrhea in cholera outbreaks, typically spread via contaminated water and food. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T85#GNS214_U1_T85_h4)

question: What is a primary environmental driver of vector-borne disease outbreaks such as malaria and yellow fever?

options.A: Overcrowded indoor classrooms without ventilation
options.B: Consumption of unpasteurized milk
options.C: Stagnant water collections and poor waste management favoring mosquito breeding
options.D: Direct contact with respiratory droplets

explanation: Stagnant water and poor waste management create ideal breeding sites for mosquito vectors, leading to surges in vector-borne diseases. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T85#GNS214_U1_T85_h4)

question: What is the primary difference between passive and active surveillance in community health nursing?

options.A: Passive surveillance involves nurses actively searching communities, while active surveillance relies on clinic visits.
options.B: Passive surveillance relies on patients reporting to the clinic, whereas active surveillance involves nurses proactively seeking out cases in the community.
options.C: Active surveillance is only used for chronic non-communicable diseases.
options.D: Passive surveillance requires laboratory confirmation for every patient.

explanation: Passive surveillance waits for patients to present at healthcare facilities, while active surveillance requires healthcare workers to actively search for cases in the community. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T85#GNS214_U1_T85_h5)

question: Which category of a case definition relies on laboratory testing for definitive verification of the pathogen?

options.A: Suspected case
options.B: Probable case
options.C: Confirmed case
options.D: Hypothetical case

explanation: A confirmed case has laboratory verification confirming the presence of the causative agent, distinguishing it from suspected and probable classifications. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T85#GNS214_U1_T85_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of constructing an epidemic curve (epi curve) during an outbreak investigation?

options.A: To calculate the total financial cost of medical treatments
options.B: To visualize the outbreak's magnitude, pattern of spread, and probable time of exposure
options.C: To replace the need for laboratory confirmation of cases
options.D: To determine the salary scale of health workers

explanation: An epi curve visually displays the timing and number of cases, helping investigators understand transmission dynamics and exposure periods. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T85#GNS214_U1_T85_h6)

question: Why is strict adherence to infection prevention and control (IPC) protocols essential during an outbreak investigation?

options.A: To reduce the paperwork required by the health ministry
options.B: To protect healthcare workers and prevent nosocomial transmission
options.C: To ensure patients pay their hospital bills on time
options.D: To eliminate the need for community education

explanation: Strict IPC protocols safeguard healthcare personnel and prevent the spread of infections within clinical and community settings. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T85#GNS214_U1_T85_h6)

question: What is the primary purpose of contact tracing during a disease outbreak?

options.A: To collect taxes from community residents
options.B: To monitor exposed persons for early signs of illness during their incubation period
options.C: To replace laboratory testing procedures
options.D: To punish individuals who fail to attend clinic appointments

explanation: Contact tracing identifies individuals who have been exposed so they can be monitored and isolated if symptoms develop, halting further spread. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T85#GNS214_U1_T85_h7)

question: Which intervention is most appropriate for environmental control during a cholera outbreak?

options.A: Mass distribution of insecticide-treated mosquito nets
options.B: Chlorination of contaminated water supplies and safe waste disposal enforcement
options.C: Prohibiting all vehicular travel between states
options.D: Administering antiretroviral therapy to all residents

explanation: Cholera is waterborne; therefore, chlorinating water sources and enforcing sanitation are vital environmental control measures. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T85#GNS214_U1_T85_h7)

question: What is the most effective approach for community health nurses to ensure health education messages reach rural populations in Nigeria?

options.A: Publishing articles exclusively in international medical journals
options.B: Using local languages, community radio, town-hall meetings, and engaging traditional leaders
options.C: Relying solely on written pamphlets distributed in English
options.D: Issuing fines for residents who do not attend lectures

explanation: Using local languages, trusted community platforms, and traditional leadership ensures messages are understood and accepted by rural populations. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T85#GNS214_U1_T85_h8)

question: Why are routine immunization programs emphasized as a core prevention strategy against outbreaks?

options.A: They completely eliminate the need for environmental sanitation.
options.B: They build community herd immunity against vaccine-preventable diseases.
options.C: They are only required during an active epidemic.
options.D: They replace the need for clinical treatment centers.

explanation: Routine immunizations establish herd immunity, protecting the community from outbreaks of vaccine-preventable infections. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T85#GNS214_U1_T85_h8)

question: Why is epidemiology important for nurses working in primary health care settings?

options.A: It helps nurses care exclusively for individual hospital patients.
options.B: It allows nurses to quantify health events and evaluate community interventions.
options.C: It eliminates the need for multidisciplinary healthcare teams.
options.D: It focuses solely on managing hospital administrative budgets.

explanation: Epidemiological terms and concepts allow primary health care nurses to quantify health events, measure disease burden, and evaluate community-level interventions. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T86#GNS214_U1_T86_h1)

question: What is a primary benefit of understanding epidemiological terms for a public health nurse in Nigeria?

options.A: Identifying vulnerable groups and allocating healthcare resources efficiently
options.B: Replacing the need for direct patient bedside care
options.C: Preventing patients from visiting secondary healthcare facilities
options.D: Automatically curing chronic communicable diseases

explanation: Mastering these terms helps nurses identify vulnerable populations and efficiently allocate limited healthcare resources for targeted interventions. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T86#GNS214_U1_T86_h1)

question: What does incidence specifically measure in a population?

options.A: The total number of all existing disease cases
options.B: The occurrence of new cases of a disease
options.C: The proportion of individuals who have died from a disease
options.D: The financial cost of treating a chronic condition

explanation: Incidence focuses strictly on counting the number of new cases of a disease that develop within a specified population over a given time period. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T86#GNS214_U1_T86_h2)

question: What is a critical requirement for individuals included when calculating the incidence of a disease?

options.A: They must already be receiving treatment in a tertiary hospital.
options.B: They must be immune to all known strains of the pathogen.
options.C: They must be initially free of the disease in question.
options.D: They must be over the age of eighteen years.

explanation: To measure new cases accurately, every individual included in the study population must be initially free of the disease being investigated. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T86#GNS214_U1_T86_h2)

question: How does incidence differ fundamentally from prevalence?

options.A: Incidence measures all existing cases, while prevalence measures only new cases.
options.B: Incidence measures new cases, while prevalence measures all existing cases.
options.C: Incidence applies only to chronic illnesses, while prevalence applies to acute illnesses.
options.D: Incidence includes deaths, while prevalence excludes deaths.

explanation: Incidence tracks the development of new cases, whereas prevalence accounts for all existing cases (both old and new) in a population at a given time. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T86#GNS214_U1_T86_h3)

question: Why is prevalence typically much higher than incidence for chronic conditions like hypertension?

options.A: Because patients live with the condition for many years, accumulating existing cases
options.B: Because hypertension spreads rapidly like an acute viral infection
options.C: Because new cases of hypertension are rarely ever recorded
options.D: Because prevalence only counts patients who are completely cured

explanation: Chronic diseases last a long time, meaning existing cases accumulate over the years, leading to a high prevalence compared to the annual rate of new cases. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T86#GNS214_U1_T86_h3)

question: What represents the denominator when calculating the standard incidence proportion?

options.A: The total number of deaths recorded in the entire country
options.B: The total number of persons at risk of developing the disease in the population
options.C: The total number of individuals who already have the chronic disease
options.D: The number of healthcare workers employed in local clinics

explanation: The denominator for incidence calculations must include only the individuals in the population who are at risk of developing the disease during the specified period. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T86#GNS214_U1_T86_h4)

question: Why is a standard multiplier (like 1,000 or 100,000) used when reporting incidence rates?

options.A: To inflate the numbers so the government allocates more funding
options.B: To convert decimal fractions into easily understandable whole numbers per population base
options.C: To account for patients who migrated out of the country
options.D: To eliminate the need for counting new cases accurately

explanation: Multipliers are used to transform small decimal values into readable whole numbers representing disease frequency per standard population size. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T86#GNS214_U1_T86_h4)

question: What is the primary characteristic of cumulative incidence?

options.A: It measures the speed of disease using person-years.
options.B: It measures the risk of developing a disease over a defined time period in a closed population.
options.C: It requires individuals to enter and leave the study at varying unpredictable times.
options.D: It calculates the total number of existing chronic cases.

explanation: Cumulative incidence represents the risk or probability of disease development over a set period, assuming all participants are followed continuously in a closed population. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T86#GNS214_U1_T86_h5)

question: When is incidence density (incidence rate) preferred over cumulative incidence?

options.A: When studying dynamic populations where individuals enter, leave, or migrate at different times
options.B: When working with a fixed group of school children who never move away
options.C: When calculating the overall prevalence of a long-term chronic condition
options.D: When it is impossible to count the number of new disease cases

explanation: Incidence density uses person-time in the denominator, making it the preferred measure for open or dynamic populations with migration or loss to follow-up. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T86#GNS214_U1_T86_h5)

question: How do environmental factors like seasonal rains and poor sanitation impact disease incidence in Nigeria?

options.A: They decrease the transmission of all known infectious diseases.
options.B: They heavily influence the incidence of waterborne and vector-borne diseases like cholera and malaria.
options.C: They prevent microorganisms from multiplying in the environment.
options.D: They eliminate the need for community health education.

explanation: Poor sanitation and seasonal changes create breeding grounds and transmission pathways that increase the incidence of diseases like cholera and malaria. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T86#GNS214_U1_T86_h6)

question: What is the direct public health consequence of low immunization coverage in a rural Nigerian community?

options.A: A decrease in the prevalence of chronic illnesses
options.B: A spike in the incidence of vaccine-preventable diseases like measles
options.C: An immediate eradication of bacterial pathogens
options.D: An increase in life expectancy among infants

explanation: Low immunization coverage leaves populations unprotected, directly resulting in an increased incidence of vaccine-preventable diseases such as measles. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T86#GNS214_U1_T86_h6)

question: What is the primary role of incidence data within a disease surveillance system?

options.A: To calculate the total number of historical deaths from decades ago
options.B: To detect early outbreaks and unusual deviations from baseline disease patterns
options.C: To determine the monthly salaries of public health nurses
options.D: To replace the need for clinical diagnosis in hospitals

explanation: Incidence data allows health authorities to monitor new cases continuously and identify outbreaks early by spotting unusual deviations from baseline patterns. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T86#GNS214_U1_T86_h7)

question: What does a declining incidence rate following a public health intervention indicate?

options.A: That the intervention or control program is succeeding
options.B: That healthcare workers have stopped reporting new cases completely
options.C: That the causative pathogen has become completely immune to treatment
options.D: That the population size has become infinitely large

explanation: A downward trend in incidence following an intervention provides clear evidence that the public health control measures are effective. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T86#GNS214_U1_T86_h7)

question: How do community health nurses in Nigeria use local incidence data at the primary care level?

options.A: To identify high-incidence zones and direct outreach teams for targeted interventions
options.B: To calculate hospital profits and manage private sector investments
options.C: To diagnose complex surgical emergencies in tertiary centers
options.D: To eliminate the requirement for community health registers

explanation: Nurses use local incidence data to spot high-risk zones and deploy outreach teams for vaccinations, distributions, and targeted health education. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T86#GNS214_U1_T86_h8)

question: Why is the aggregation of incidence data from primary health centers important for national bodies like the NCDC?

options.A: It allows national agencies to deploy resources and emergency response teams to high-risk areas.
options.B: It proves that infectious diseases no longer exist in the country.
options.C: It removes all responsibilities from local state health ministries.
options.D: It replaces clinical treatment guidelines with statistical charts.

explanation: Aggregated incidence data helps national bodies like the NCDC see the bigger picture and direct medical supplies and response teams to areas with high transmission risk. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T86#GNS214_U1_T86_h8)

question: What primary factor facilitates the rapid spread of communicable diseases in under-resourced communities?

options.A: High literacy rates
options.B: Poor sanitation and inadequate potable water
options.C: Advanced diagnostic technology
options.D: Abundant healthcare staffing

explanation: Poor sanitation and a lack of clean, potable water create an environment where pathogens thrive and easily spread among vulnerable populations. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h1)

question: Which of the following populations is generally considered most vulnerable to the severe impacts of communicable diseases?

options.A: Middle-aged corporate workers
options.B: Children under five and pregnant women
options.C: Retired military personnel
options.D: Healthy adult males

explanation: Children under five and pregnant women have developing or altered immune systems, making them particularly susceptible to severe complications from infectious illnesses. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h1)

question: How is an epidemic best defined in epidemiological terms?

options.A: A disease constantly present at a low level in a specific area
options.B: An unexpected sudden increase in disease cases above normal expectations
options.C: A disease that only affects animals and never humans
options.D: The total number of existing cases in a population

explanation: An epidemic represents a sudden spike or surge in disease incidence that surpasses the baseline level normally anticipated within that population. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h2)

question: What does the incidence rate of a communicable disease measure?

options.A: The total number of existing cases at a single point in time
options.B: The number of new cases developing over a specific time period
options.C: The total number of deaths caused by the disease
options.D: The rate at which a pathogen mutates in a host

explanation: Incidence specifically tracks newly diagnosed cases arising within a population over a defined timeframe, showing ongoing transmission rates. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h2)

question: In the chain of infection, what does the reservoir represent?

options.A: The method by which the pathogen travels
options.B: The natural habitat where the pathogen lives and multiplies
options.C: The specific medication used to treat the infection
options.D: The immune response of the infected person

explanation: The reservoir is where the infectious agent naturally lives, grows, and multiplies, which can include humans, animals, or environmental sources. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h3)

question: What is the primary purpose of nursing interventions like hand hygiene in relation to the chain of infection?

options.A: To create a new reservoir for pathogens
options.B: To increase host susceptibility
options.C: To interrupt or break links in the chain of infection
options.D: To alter the portal of exit of the host

explanation: Infection control measures like hand hygiene are specifically implemented to break the chain of infection and prevent pathogen transmission. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h3)

question: Which of the following is an example of indirect transmission via a fomite?

options.A: Sexual intercourse with an infected partner
options.B: Direct skin-to-skin touching during wrestling
options.C: Handling contaminated bedding or medical instruments
options.D: Inhaling large droplets expelled close to an infected person's face

explanation: Fomites are inanimate objects, such as bedding and medical instruments, that transfer pathogens indirectly to a new host. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h4)

question: What type of transmission is involved when malaria is spread to a human via a mosquito bite?

options.A: Airborne transmission
options.B: Vector-borne transmission
options.C: Direct droplet transmission
options.D: Vehicle-borne transmission

explanation: Living organisms like mosquitoes that carry and transmit infectious pathogens are classified as vectors, making this vector-borne transmission. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h4)

question: Which parasite and vector are responsible for transmitting malaria in Nigeria?

options.A: Mycobacterium tuberculosis and houseflies
options.B: Plasmodium parasites and female Anopheles mosquitoes
options.C: Vibrio cholerae and contaminated water
options.D: Lassa virus and multimammate rats

explanation: Malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites and is transmitted specifically through the bite of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h5)

question: What is the primary mode of transmission for Tuberculosis (TB)?

options.A: Airborne droplets
options.B: Vector bites
options.C: Contaminated water ingestion
options.D: Direct contact with rat urine

explanation: Tuberculosis is an airborne bacterial infection spread when an infected person coughs or sneezes, releasing bacilli into the air. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h5)

question: What is an essential component to explore during the health history of a patient suspected of having a communicable disease?

options.A: Patient's favorite recreational hobbies
options.B: Recent travel history and contact with sick individuals
options.C: Family financial background and assets
options.D: Patient's architectural preferences

explanation: Recent travel and contact history provide vital clues regarding potential exposure to specific infectious agents and help narrow down differential diagnoses. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h6)

question: When collecting diagnostic specimens for a suspected communicable disease, what primary precaution must the nurse observe?

options.A: Ensure specimens are collected without gloves to improve dexterity
options.B: Adhere strictly to universal precautions for safe collection and transport
options.C: Delay labeling until the end of the shift
options.D: Store all samples at room temperature indefinitely

explanation: Adhering to universal precautions protects both the healthcare worker and prevents contamination of the sample during collection and transport. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h6)

question: Which of the following activities is classified as a primary prevention strategy for communicable diseases?

options.A: Screening asymptomatic individuals for high blood pressure
options.B: Routine childhood immunization and vaccination programs
options.C: Administering antibiotics to cure an active infection
options.D: Providing physical therapy to stroke survivors

explanation: Immunization and vaccination are primary prevention measures designed to prevent individuals from contracting the disease in the first place. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h7)

question: What is the primary goal of tertiary prevention in infectious disease management?

options.A: To stop the disease from ever occurring
options.B: To detect the disease in its earliest asymptomatic stage
options.C: To minimize disability and manage established disease complications
options.D: To replace all routine community sanitation projects

explanation: Tertiary prevention focuses on rehabilitation, managing existing complications, and reducing long-term disability or death from an established condition. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h7)

question: What is a major responsibility of a nurse participating in epidemiological surveillance at the primary health care level?

options.A: Prescribing surgical procedures for chronic conditions
options.B: Identifying unusual disease clusters and reporting them promptly
options.C: Conducting international travel restrictions
options.D: Manufacturing pharmaceuticals locally

explanation: Surveillance involves monitoring health trends and promptly reporting unusual disease clusters to public health authorities to initiate timely outbreak responses. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h8)

question: Why is community mobilization by nurses essential in primary health care disease control programs?

options.A: To replace the need for medical doctors entirely
options.B: To foster trust, dispel health myths, and encourage local participation
options.C: To enforce strict fines on individuals who fall ill
options.D: To collect taxes for hospital construction

explanation: Community mobilization helps build local trust, addresses cultural misconceptions, and drives active participation in health interventions like immunization drives. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T87#GNS214_U1_T87_h8)

question: What defines an endemic disease within a specific population or region?

options.A: It appears suddenly and affects the entire global population.
options.B: It is constantly present at a predictable baseline rate within that area.
options.C: It occurs only once every decade in a localized community.
options.D: It has been completely eradicated from the region.

explanation: An endemic disease is characterized by its constant presence and predictable baseline rate of occurrence within a specific geographic area over time. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T88#GNS214_U1_T88_h1)

question: Why is it important for a nurse to understand the baseline endemic level of a disease?

options.A: To know when normal baseline cases are being exceeded and require intervention
options.B: To ensure the disease spreads faster to build herd immunity
options.C: To eliminate the need for any public health reporting
options.D: To prove that the disease is entirely harmless

explanation: Knowing the baseline level helps nurses and public health authorities recognize when case numbers surge beyond normal limits, signaling a potential outbreak. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T88#GNS214_U1_T88_h1)

question: How does an epidemic differ from an endemic disease?

options.A: An epidemic is constantly present at a low level, while an endemic disease appears suddenly.
options.B: An epidemic is a sudden, unexpected surge in cases above the normal baseline.
options.C: An epidemic only affects animals, whereas endemic diseases affect humans.
options.D: There is no clinical difference between the two terms.

explanation: An epidemic is characterized by a sudden and unexpected increase in the number of disease cases well above the normal baseline expected for that community. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T88#GNS214_U1_T88_h2)

question: What primary feature distinguishes a pandemic from an epidemic?

options.A: A pandemic crosses international borders and affects a global population.
options.B: A pandemic only occurs during the dry season.
options.C: A pandemic has a much lower mortality rate than an epidemic.
options.D: A pandemic is confined to a single rural village.

explanation: A pandemic is an epidemic that has spread extensively across international borders, impacting a large portion of the global population. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T88#GNS214_U1_T88_h2)

question: What are the three core components of the epidemiological triangle?

options.A: Doctor, Nurse, Patient
options.B: Agent, Host, Environment
options.C: Vector, Vaccine, Hospital
options.D: Infection, Immunity, Death

explanation: The epidemiological triangle consists of the agent, the host, and the environment, which interact to influence disease occurrence. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T88#GNS214_U1_T88_h3)

question: In the context of malaria as an endemic disease, what role does the human population play?

options.A: The agent
options.B: The environment
options.C: The host
options.D: The vector

explanation: The human population serves as the host that harbors the infectious agent and whose susceptibility affects disease dynamics. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T88#GNS214_U1_T88_h3)

question: Which demographic group is most vulnerable to the severe effects of endemic malaria in Nigeria?

options.A: Elderly males above 70 years
options.B: Pregnant women and children under five years
options.C: Adolescent school children
options.D: Adult healthcare workers

explanation: Pregnant women and children under five years of age are particularly vulnerable to the severe morbidity and mortality caused by endemic malaria. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T88#GNS214_U1_T88_h4)

question: What is a primary transmission route for typhoid fever in endemic communities?

options.A: Inhalation of airborne respiratory droplets
options.B: Ingestion of food and water contaminated with Salmonella typhi
options.C: Bites from infected Anopheles mosquitoes
options.D: Direct skin contact with contaminated soil

explanation: Typhoid fever is primarily transmitted through the ingestion of food and water that has been contaminated with Salmonella typhi bacteria. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T88#GNS214_U1_T88_h4)

question: Which of the following is a key environmental factor that sustains endemic vector-borne diseases?

options.A: Advanced industrial air conditioning
options.B: Inadequate waste management and heavy rainfall creating vector breeding sites
options.C: High levels of nationwide vaccination coverage
options.D: Strict enforcement of building safety codes

explanation: Inadequate waste management and heavy seasonal rainfall create standing water and breeding sites that sustain vector-borne endemic diseases. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T88#GNS214_U1_T88_h5)

question: How do socioeconomic challenges like poverty and poor housing contribute to endemicity?

options.A: They ensure complete immunity against all infections.
options.B: They create conditions where infectious agents circulate continuously among vulnerable people.
options.C: They eliminate the need for community health workers.
options.D: They guarantee immediate access to specialized hospital care.

explanation: Poverty and poor housing foster environments that facilitate the continuous circulation and transmission of infectious agents. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T88#GNS214_U1_T88_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of disease surveillance in public health nursing?

options.A: To punish healthcare facilities that report high infection rates
options.B: The systematic collection and analysis of health data to guide public health action
options.C: To replace clinical nursing care with administrative paperwork
options.D: To advertise pharmaceutical products in rural communities

explanation: Disease surveillance involves the systematic collection and analysis of health data, which is essential for planning, monitoring, and executing public health interventions. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T88#GNS214_U1_T88_h6)

question: How do frontline PHC nurses contribute to the national Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) system?

options.A: By accurately recording diagnoses and reporting unusual case clusters from local clinics
options.B: By independently manufacturing vaccines for endemic diseases
options.C: By restricting patient access to local health posts
options.D: By treating patients without documenting their symptoms

explanation: Nurses contribute by meticulously recording clinical cases and reporting unusual spikes or clusters to higher public health authorities. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T88#GNS214_U1_T88_h6)

question: Which intervention represents a specific protection measure against endemic malaria at the community level?

options.A: Administering intravenous antibiotics to all community members
options.B: Distributing and promoting the use of insecticide-treated bed nets
options.C: Closing down all local water bodies
options.D: Isolating patients with chronic hypertension

explanation: Insecticide-treated bed nets provide specific protection by preventing mosquito bites and subsequent malaria transmission. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T88#GNS214_U1_T88_h7)

question: Why is community participation emphasized in PHC prevention and control strategies?

options.A: It ensures that interventions are culturally relevant, accepted, and actively sustained by the population.
options.B: It relieves nurses of all clinical responsibilities.
options.C: It prevents the government from spending any money on healthcare.
options.D: It eliminates the need for rapid diagnostic tests.

explanation: Involving the community ensures that health initiatives align with local values, fostering high adoption rates and sustainable disease control. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T88#GNS214_U1_T88_h7)

question: Which term describes a disease that is constantly present at a usual prevalence within a specific geographic area?

options.A: Pandemic
options.B: Epidemic
options.C: Endemic
options.D: Sporadic

explanation: An endemic disease refers to the constant presence or usual prevalence of a disease within a given geographic area or population group. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T89#GNS214_U1_T89_h1)

question: How does an outbreak differ typically from a full-scale epidemic in terms of scope?

options.A: An outbreak only affects animals.
options.B: An outbreak is usually confined to a more limited geographic area or localized cluster.
options.C: An outbreak lasts for exactly one year.
options.D: An outbreak implies zero mortality.

explanation: An outbreak carries the same definition as an epidemic but is often used to describe a more limited geographic area or a localized cluster of cases. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T89#GNS214_U1_T89_h1)

question: In the epidemiological triangle, what does the 'host' represent?

options.A: The climatic condition of the area
options.B: The human or animal that harbors the infectious agent
options.C: The biological toxin or virus
options.D: The vector control program

explanation: The host is defined as the human or animal that harbors the infectious agent, whose susceptibility is influenced by various personal factors. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T89#GNS214_U1_T89_h2)

question: Which of the following is considered an environmental factor in the epidemiological triangle?

options.A: Genetic makeup of the patient
options.B: Virulence of the viral strain
options.C: Sanitation infrastructure and water supply
options.D: Antibiotic resistance profile

explanation: The environment encompasses external factors such as housing conditions, sanitation infrastructure, and water supply that affect exposure opportunities. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T89#GNS214_U1_T89_h2)

question: Which seasonal factor is typically associated with outbreaks of Lassa fever in Nigeria?

options.A: The rainy season
options.B: The dry season
options.C: The harmattan dust storms exclusively
options.D: Winter solstice

explanation: Lassa fever tends to peak during the dry season as interactions with rodent reservoirs increase. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T89#GNS214_U1_T89_h3)

question: What characterizes a propagated outbreak compared to a common-source outbreak?

options.A: It spreads directly from person to person.
options.B: It arises from a single contaminated water well.
options.C: It is exclusively caused by animal vectors.
options.D: It only occurs in cold weather.

explanation: Propagated outbreaks spread from person to person, whereas common-source outbreaks stem from a shared exposure like contaminated water. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T89#GNS214_U1_T89_h3)

question: Which of the following represents an example of indirect transmission via a vector?

options.A: Direct skin-to-skin contact with a measles rash
options.B: Inhalation of droplet nuclei from a cough
options.C: Transmission of Lassa fever virus via rodents
options.D: Sexual intercourse transmitting an infection

explanation: Vectors are living organisms like rodents or mosquitoes that transmit infectious agents to humans, making rat-borne Lassa fever an example of vector/reservoir indirect transmission. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T89#GNS214_U1_T89_h4)

question: What is a primary environmental risk factor contributing to waterborne epidemic diseases like cholera?

options.A: High vaccination rates
options.B: Inadequate access to safe drinking water and poor sanitation
options.C: Strict adherence to hand hygiene
options.D: Low population density

explanation: Inadequate access to potable water and poor sanitation are primary risk factors that facilitate the spread of waterborne epidemics like cholera. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T89#GNS214_U1_T89_h4)

question: What is the primary purpose of the Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) strategy in healthcare facilities?

options.A: To provide financial loans to patients
options.B: To systematically collect, analyze, and report health data for priority diseases
options.C: To manage hospital kitchen inventories
options.D: To schedule nursing shift rosters

explanation: Disease surveillance involves the ongoing collection, analysis, and interpretation of health data to plan and evaluate public health responses, as structured by the IDSR. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T89#GNS214_U1_T89_h5)

question: Who should a primary health care nurse immediately notify upon identifying a suspected case of an epidemic-prone disease?

options.A: The hospital catering department
options.B: The local government area Disease Surveillance and Notification Officer (DSNO)
options.C: The international news media
options.D: The pharmaceutical manufacturing plant

explanation: Suspected cases must be reported immediately through formal channels to the local government area Disease Surveillance and Notification Officer (DSNO) to trigger a rapid public health response. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T89#GNS214_U1_T89_h5)

question: What is a primary objective of establishing dedicated isolation units during an active epidemic?

options.A: To reduce hospital utility bills
options.B: To prevent nosocomial (hospital-acquired) spread to other patients and staff
options.C: To isolate the healthcare facility from the government
options.D: To eliminate the need for hand hygiene

explanation: Case management in dedicated isolation units is crucial to prevent nosocomial spread and protect other vulnerable patients and healthcare workers. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T89#GNS214_U1_T89_h6)

question: Why is contact tracing an essential component of outbreak management?

options.A: It tracks financial donations made to the clinic.
options.B: It monitors exposed individuals during their incubation period to catch new cases early.
options.C: It helps in scheduling nursing annual leave.
options.D: It replaces the need for laboratory testing.

explanation: Contact tracing involves monitoring exposed individuals during their incubation period so that new infections can be identified and isolated promptly. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T89#GNS214_U1_T89_h6)

question: What is a key strategy for a nurse when addressing rumors and fear during a community epidemic?

options.A: Ignoring the community concerns completely
options.B: Engaging the community with cultural sensitivity, empathy, and clear communication
options.C: Enforcing strict punitive measures against anyone who asks questions
options.D: Relying solely on written pamphlets in a foreign language

explanation: Nurses must engage communities with cultural sensitivity, empathy, and clear communication in local dialects to build trust and dispel misinformation. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T89#GNS214_U1_T89_h7)

question: Which of the following best describes the broader advocacy role of a nurse during public health outbreaks?

options.A: Limiting patient access to health education
options.B: Advocating for improved water, sanitation infrastructure, and health resources
options.C: Discouraging community leaders from participating in health meetings
options.D: Focusing exclusively on hospital administrative tasks

explanation: Nurses advocate for policy changes, improved water and sanitation infrastructure, and adequate resource allocation to strengthen community health systems. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T89#GNS214_U1_T89_h7)

question: What is the primary focus of disease control in public health?

options.A: Completely eliminating all diseases globally within a week
options.B: Reducing disease incidence, prevalence, morbidity, and mortality to acceptable levels
options.C: Focusing solely on hospital-based surgical interventions
options.D: Increasing the cost of healthcare services for rural dwellers

explanation: Disease control focuses on reducing the burden of diseases in terms of incidence, prevalence, morbidity, and mortality to an acceptable public health level through various interventions. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T90#GNS214_U1_T90_h1)

question: Why is public health nursing considered vital in disease control within Nigeria?

options.A: Nurses only work in private intensive care units
options.B: Nurses implement preventive measures, educate the populace, and manage health crises at the grassroots
options.C: Nurses are solely responsible for manufacturing vaccines
options.D: Nurses dictate national economic policies

explanation: Public health nurses play an indispensable role by executing preventive measures, educating communities, and managing health crises right at the grassroots level. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T90#GNS214_U1_T90_h1)

question: How does 'incidence' differ from 'prevalence' in epidemiological terms?

options.A: Incidence measures total existing cases, while prevalence measures only new cases
options.B: Incidence measures new cases over a given period, while prevalence measures total existing cases at a specific point in time
options.C: Incidence and prevalence mean the exact same thing
options.D: Prevalence only applies to non-communicable diseases

explanation: Incidence specifically refers to the number of new cases arising over a period, whereas prevalence accounts for all existing cases (both old and new) at a specific time. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T90#GNS214_U1_T90_h2)

question: What are the three components of the epidemiological triad?

options.A: Doctor, nurse, and patient
options.B: Hospital, clinic, and pharmacy
options.C: Agent, host, and environment
options.D: Vaccine, antibiotic, and immunity

explanation: The epidemiological triad consists of the agent, the host, and the environment, which interact dynamically to influence the occurrence and spread of diseases. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T90#GNS214_U1_T90_h2)

question: What distinguishes disease 'elimination' from disease 'eradication'?

options.A: Elimination means zero worldwide cases, while eradication means zero cases in a single hospital
options.B: Elimination is zero incidence in a defined geographic area with ongoing prevention needed, whereas eradication is worldwide permanent reduction to zero
options.C: Eradication requires no vaccination, while elimination requires lifelong medication
options.D: There is no difference between the two terms

explanation: Elimination refers to reducing incidence to zero within a specific geographic area requiring continued intervention, while eradication means the disease has been permanently reduced to zero globally. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T90#GNS214_U1_T90_h3)

question: Which of the following diseases is cited as a prime historic example of eradication?

options.A: Malaria
options.B: Tuberculosis
options.C: Smallpox
options.D: Cholera

explanation: Smallpox is the classic historic example of a disease that has been successfully eradicated worldwide. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T90#GNS214_U1_T90_h3)

question: Which activity represents primary prevention in disease control?

options.A: Administering routine childhood immunizations against measles
options.B: Treating complications of chronic kidney disease
options.C: Conducting blood pressure screening for early hypertension detection
options.D: Physiotherapy rehabilitation for a stroke patient

explanation: Routine childhood immunization is a primary prevention strategy aimed at preventing the onset of disease before it occurs. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T90#GNS214_U1_T90_h4)

question: What is the primary objective of secondary prevention?

options.A: Preventing the initial exposure to a pathogen
options.B: Early diagnosis and prompt treatment to halt disease progression
